exp.7:5:
Esther tells the king that she cannot remain looking on while her people suffer. With grief, she asks how she could bear to see the disaster and ruin of her family and her people. Here "people" refers to her relatives, her Jewish people.

Queen Esther had already come before King Ahasuerus. Haman had obtained a decree to destroy the Jews, and although Haman had already been hanged, that order was still in force. Esther asks that it be overturned, because a king's law could not simply be cancelled.

For today: when someone we love suffers an injustice, we cannot look the other way. If God has given us a voice, influence, or resources, we can use them with respect and courage to help, to pray, and to act on behalf of others.
exp.8:17:
This verse tells that the Jews of Shushan, the capital of the Persian kingdom, gathered together on the thirteenth and fourteenth days of the month of Adar to defend themselves against their enemies. On the fifteenth day they rested and made it a day of feasting and gladness. The word "Shushan" is the city of Susa, and "assembled together" means that they organized themselves and came together.

Here the narrator of the book of Esther speaks. He describes how the danger that threatened the Jewish people because of Haman's decree came to an end. The Jews in the provinces rested on the fourteenth day, but those in Shushan fought one more day and rested on the fifteenth. That is why the feast of Purim is celebrated on different dates depending on the place, as the text that follows explains.

For today: after a struggle or a difficult trial, God invites us to rest and give thanks. Taking time to celebrate what he has done helps us remember his faithfulness.
exp.4:6:
This verse says that Esther speaks up to answer the king. "Petition" and "request" are almost synonyms: both refer to what she wants to ask of him. It is as if she were saying, "This is what I want to ask you." But the request itself comes in the next verse.

Esther is at the banquet she prepared for King Ahasuerus and Haman. The king has already offered her up to half the kingdom. She does not respond right away with her great request, but takes one more step: she invites them to a second banquet. The Bible does not explain her reasons; some think she was looking for the right moment, but this is only an interpretation.

For today: not everything is resolved in a hurry. Sometimes it is wise to pray, wait, and act with prudence, trusting that God guides the right moment.
exp.3:6:
Mordecai told him everything that had happened to him. He also informed him of the sum of silver that Haman had promised to pay into the king's treasuries in order to have the Jews destroyed.

Esther, who was queen but did not yet know the gravity of what had occurred, sends Hathach, a trusted eunuch, to find out why Mordecai was in mourning. Mordecai answers with concrete facts: what had happened and the money Haman had offered. In this way Esther could understand that this was not a simple problem, but a real threat against her people.

For today: when we face a difficult situation or ask for help, it is good to speak with clarity and truth, without exaggerating or hiding anything. Honest information helps others understand and act with wisdom.
exp.4:1:
In this verse, King Ahasuerus saw Queen Esther standing in the inner court of the palace, and he was pleased with her. So he held out the golden scepter that he had in his hand, and Esther came near and touched its tip.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. According to chapter 4, Esther came in without being called, and that could cost her her life. The extended scepter was a sign that the king accepted her. She was doing this to ask for help for her people, the Jews, who were under threat.

For today: when you have to take a hard step for the good of others, prepare yourself, pray, and act with respect and courage. You do not know how others will respond, but God can open doors that seemed closed.
exp.3:8:
This verse says that Hatach went back to Esther and reported to her everything Mordecai had said. The phrase "Hatach went back" and the word "reported" carry the meaning of bringing her the message. In the text her name appears as Esther, and the Mordecai in this passage is the one we now call Mordecai, so the names are the same ones readers already know.

Hatach was a servant of the king whom Esther had sent to find out why Mordecai was dressed in mourning. Mordecai, Esther's cousin and guardian, sent her word of the decree that threatened the Jews. Hatach acted as the messenger between the two, because Esther could not go out to speak with him herself. This is the step before the difficult decision she must now make.

For today: sometimes God uses ordinary people who carry a message faithfully. We can be like Hatach: passing on honestly what others need to hear, and opening the way for someone to act with courage.
exp.5:7:
Haman tells the king what should be done for the man the king wishes to honor. He proposes that they bring the royal apparel the king wears, the horse the king rides, and the royal crown that is set upon his head. Today we would say "robe" or "cloak" instead of "apparel". Some scholars understand that the crown was placed on the horse, and others that it was placed on the man; the text does not make this completely clear.

Haman speaks because the king asks him, and he believes the honor is for himself. Out of pride, he asks for the most. But the king orders that all of this be done for Mordecai, the Jew whom Haman hated.

For today: pride deceives us and makes us believe that everything revolves around us. Let us ask God for a humble heart, one that rejoices when others are honored.
exp.0:20:
This verse says that Memucan's proposal pleased King Ahasuerus and his princes, and that the king put it into practice. The word "pleased" here means that the proposal was welcome to them and seemed good in their eyes. The phrase "the word of Memucan" refers to what Memucan had said, that is, his counsel.

The context is this: Queen Vashti had refused to appear before the king during a banquet. Memucan, one of the counselors, feared that other women would follow her example and proposed removing her from her position. His advice came from anger and from fear of losing authority, not from a search for justice. The Bible here recounts what happened without approving of it.

For today: before accepting advice, let us ask what motivates it. Decisions made out of pride or anger, even when they please many people, can cause harm. Let us seek the wisdom of God, which is humble and peaceable (James 3:17).
exp.8:10:
That same day, the king Ahasuerus was told how many had been killed in Shushan, the capital, where he lived. The place where the king lived, meaning his palace and main city, is what the verse refers to here. A count, meaning a report or record, is what was brought to him.

The speaker here is not a character but the narrator of the book. The Jews defended themselves against those who wanted to destroy them, according to the decree that Haman had promoted. Haman's ten sons were killed, and the text stresses that the Jews did not take the plunder. This shows that they were acting in self-defense and not for gain. The report to the king opens the conversation with Esther.

For today: when you have to defend what is right, do it with clean motives. Do not let yourself be moved by personal profit, revenge, or the desire to get ahead, but by care for life and for the truth.
exp.0:0:
This verse opens the book of Esther by placing the story in the time of King Ahasuerus. It makes clear that this is the king who ruled from India to Ethiopia over one hundred and twenty-seven provinces. The word "came to pass" means "happened." "Provinces" were regions governed within the empire.

The author of the book is not named, and it is not known with certainty who wrote it. It tells the events as a historical account. Many believe Ahasuerus is the Persian king known as Xerxes I, though this is suggested mainly by the similarity of names. The text highlights his enormous power as the setting for what follows: a vast empire in which the Jewish people lived in exile.

Although God is not mentioned directly in this book, we can learn that He works even within the great systems of human power. If today you feel small in the face of enormous situations, remember that God is not absent. You can trust that He continues to guide your story, even when you cannot clearly see His hand.
exp.0:6:
This verse tells that at the banquet of King Ahasuerus they served the drink in golden cups, and each cup was different from the others. There was also plenty of wine that was "royal," that is, the very wine of the palace, and it was served in abundance, according to the king's generosity. The phrase "gave them drink" means "they served them," and "according to the king's means" means "according to the king's resources and power."

The author of the book describes here the feast that Ahasuerus (also called Xerxes in other languages) held in Susa, the capital. No one speaks; it is the narrator who shows the enormous wealth of the king. Many understand that the account sets the scene for what follows: a kingdom full of power and luxury, but also of pride. God is not named in the book, although his care becomes visible later on.

For today: wealth and spectacle are impressive, but they are not the most valuable things. Let us ask God for a grateful and generous heart, one that uses what it has to bless others and not to show off.
exp.0:1:
This verse says that in those days, King Ahasuerus sat on the throne of his kingdom, and that the throne was in Shushan, the capital. The phrase "after he had settled" is an old way of saying "once he was firmly established on his throne." Here "throne" means the seat of the king's authority.

The book of Esther is told by a narrator who does not identify himself. Here he sets the scene: a very powerful king, with an enormous government and a palace in Shushan. Many believe Ahasuerus is Xerxes I of Persia, although the text does not say so in those words. This introduction prepares the story that follows, in which God will act without being named directly.

For today: even when human power seems vast and secure, it does not have the final word. We can trust that God works with care even when we do not see it at first glance.
exp.7:2:
This verse tells that Esther came again before King Ahasuerus. She fell at his feet, wept, and begged him to put away the evil that Haman the Agagite had planned against the Jews. The sentence about the old wording is removed here since the reader's verse uses "devised" and "mischief," which already carry that meaning.

Haman had already been punished, and his property had been given to Esther. But the decree he had made to destroy the Jews was still in force. Esther was no longer speaking only for her own life, but for her whole people. That is why she insists with tears and humility. According to the following text, the king extends the golden scepter to her, and she then makes her formal request.

For today: when something hurts you because of what happens to others, do not stay silent or indifferent. Pray and act with humility and courage, even if you have already had a personal victory. God can use your voice to help many people.
exp.3:12:
Mordecai tells Esther not to imagine that she will be safe just because she lives in the king's palace. The phrase "think not with yourself" is rewritten here as "do not imagine in your heart" in plain terms, meaning she should not picture herself as exempt from danger. He warns her that if the decree of destruction is carried out, she would not escape any more than the other Jews.

Esther had just explained that going in to the king without being called could cost her her life. Mordecai, her cousin who raised her, answers her firmly. A decree threatened all the Jews in the kingdom, and he urges her to act. His message is harsh, but it comes from love and from the urgency of the moment.

For today: do not hide behind your comfort or your position when others are suffering and you are able to help. Ask God for courage and wisdom to use your place, your voice, or your influence on behalf of others, even when it involves risk.
exp.4:9:
Esther 5:10 says that Haman held back and did nothing against Mordecai at that moment. He went home and sent for his friends and his wife Zeresh. The word for "held himself back" means he controlled himself or restrained himself. The phrase "sent and called for" means he had them brought together to gather around him.

The narrator tells what happens after Esther invited Haman to a banquet with the king. Haman left happy, but he was filled with rage when he saw that Mordecai would not bow down before him. Although he restrained himself, his anger was still alive. He looks to vent to his family and friends, where he will boast of his riches and his honor.

For today: holding back anger is not the same as healing it. Haman kept quiet, but his pride kept growing. When something bothers us, let us bring it to God in prayer and seek wise counsel, not from those who only feed our pride.
exp.8:16:
This verse says that the thirteenth day of the month Adar was the day when the Jews in the provinces defended themselves against their enemies. The next day, the fourteenth, they rested and made it a day of feasting and gladness. The word "rested" in the verse means they stopped and took a break, and "made it" means they turned that day into a celebration.

Here the narrator of the book of Esther tells how God protected his people in the Persian empire. A decree had ordered the Jews destroyed, but another decree allowed them to defend themselves. Once the threat had passed, they rested and celebrated. The verses that follow explain that the people of Susa celebrated a day later, on the fifteenth, and that is why there were two dates of celebration. This is connected to the origin of the feast of Purim.

For today: when God brings us out of a difficult trial, it is good to stop, rest, give thanks, and celebrate with others. Sharing joy with family and friends helps us remember his care for us.
exp.8:9:
This verse ends the list of the ten sons of Haman, who died on the day the Jews defended themselves. They are called the sons of Haman, the son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews. And one thing stands out: they did not lay their hand on the spoil, that is, they did not take the possessions of the dead. The word "spoil" means plunder.

The narrator of the book tells how the king's decree allowing the Jews to defend themselves was carried out. Haman had planned to destroy them. The Jews did not act for gain, but for defense. This is repeated three times in the chapter, and so it seems important to the author. Taking plunder would have shown greed, and the text emphasizes that there was none.

For today: even when we are right or defending something just, let us watch our motives. Let us not use difficult situations to gain something for ourselves.
exp.8:20:
This verse says that Mordecai commanded the Jews to observe every year the fourteenth day and the fifteenth day of the month of Adar. "Ordering them" means giving them the instruction to do it, and "observe" means to remember it with a feast.

The narrator tells what Mordecai did after the Jews were saved from Haman's plan to destroy them. Mordecai wrote letters to all the provinces of King Ahasuerus's kingdom. Some Jews kept the fourteenth day and others the fifteenth, depending on whether they lived in villages or in walled cities. With this order the aim was to unify the date and keep alive the memory of that deliverance. This is the basis of the feast of Purim.

For today: take some time to remember with gratitude the times God sustained you in difficult moments. You can write them down or share them with your family, and help someone in need, as Mordecai urged.
exp.2:8:
Haman asks the king to sign a decree to destroy the Jews. He offers to pay ten thousand talents of silver, an enormous sum, to the men in charge of the king's finances, so that the money will reach the royal treasury.

Haman, a senior official of King Ahasuerus, speaks here. He had already accused the Jews of being different and of not obeying the king. Behind his plan lie hatred and ambition. The text calls him the enemy of the Jews, and he tries to buy the king's decision with money.

For today: be wary of anyone who accuses a whole group of people with broad generalizations and offers money or power as the solution. Ask God for courage to defend the wronged and to speak the truth when others stay silent.
exp.1:18:
When the young women were gathered together a second time, Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate. The word "virgins" here refers to the young women gathered for the palace. "Was sitting" means that he had a place or position there.

It is the narrator of the book who speaks. Esther is already queen, but Mordecai still remains close to the palace. Scholars do not fully agree on why there was a second gathering of young women. It is also not certain what his exact role at the gate was; many think he held some official position, since the gate was a place where legal matters were handled. What follows shows that he was paying attention to what was happening.

For today: God can work through people who remain faithful in their place, without seeking applause. Mordecai did not take advantage of Esther being queen. He keeps doing his work with constancy. You too can serve faithfully where you are, trusting that God sees and uses what is simple.
exp.2:6:
This verse tells that, in the first month of the twelfth year of King Ahasuerus, Haman had lots cast, called "Pur," meaning the lot, as if they were dice or stones. He did this day after day and month after month, to choose a date. The lot fell on the twelfth month, called Adar.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Haman was filled with rage because Mordecai would not bow down to him. So he sought to destroy all the Jews in the kingdom. To decide when to do it, he used the lot, as was done in that culture to seek a favorable time.

For today: hatred can plan with great care, but it does not have the last word. Haman left his plan to chance, but God continues to guide the story. Entrust your worries to God and not to chance.
exp.8:0:
It says that on the thirteenth day of the month of Adar, the twelfth month of the Jewish calendar, the time came for the king's decree to be carried out. On that day, the enemies of the Jews expected to gain control over them, but the opposite happened: the Jews gained the upper hand over those who hated them.

The narrator of the book of Esther is speaking. Earlier, Haman had obtained a decree to destroy the Jews throughout the empire. Afterward, Esther and Mordecai obtained another decree that allowed them to defend themselves. This verse shows the turn of the story: what seemed to be a sentence of death ended in protection.

For today: when a situation seems hopeless, do not give up or act in despair. Pray, seek wise counsel, and do what is yours to do with courage and honesty. Although God is not named in Esther, his care is seen in the outcome.
exp.8:15:
The verse tells that the other Jews who lived in the king's provinces, far from the capital, also gathered together to defend their lives. They gained rest from their enemies and killed seventy-five thousand of their adversaries. Even so, they took nothing from the plunder. The phrase "they laid not their hands on the prey" means that they did not take advantage of the spoils.

The speaker is the narrator of the book of Esther. Haman had planned to destroy the Jews, and the king allowed them to defend themselves. The account stresses that they acted to survive and not for gain. Some scholars see in this a sign that their motive was not greed.

For today: when we defend what is right, let us guard our hearts. We can act with firmness without seeking personal benefit. Let us ask ourselves: "Am I seeking justice or my own advantage?"
exp.2:0:
After these things, King Ahasuerus advanced Haman, the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, and raised his position, setting his seat above all the princes who were with him. This verse tells us that the king gave Haman a great promotion, honoring him and giving him power and authority, and that Haman was placed in the highest position, above the other officials of the kingdom.

Here the narrator of the book simply reports the events. Esther does not explain why the king chose Haman. What follows shows that this promotion sets up the conflict with Mordecai, who did not bow down to him. That Haman is described as an Agagite could point to a link with Agag, king of the Amalekites, an ancient enemy of Israel, though some scholars debate how much weight that detail carries.

For today: power and applause can grow very quickly, but they do not make anyone good. Let us ask God for humility so that we do not depend on human recognition.
exp.1:1:
These are the words of the king's servants, the officials who attended him. They gave him a proposal: that young unmarried women be sought out, who were lovely to look at, so that he could choose among them.

The one speaking is the group of advisers of King Ahasuerus (Xerxes). His anger at Queen Vashti had already cooled, but she had been removed from her position, and the king kept remembering what had happened. The advisers suggested a remedy: look for a new queen. Here the Bible simply reports the events; it neither approves nor condemns this system, which today strikes us as unjust to women.

For today: before acting on impulse or pain, it is wise to pause and seek wise counsel. And even when the decisions of others are unjust, God can work within them, as the story of Esther will show.
exp.8:5:
This verse tells that in Shushan, the capital of the Persian kingdom, the Jews killed five hundred men. The word "Shushan" is the city of Susa, and "destroyed" here means they put an end to them. These were men who had made themselves enemies of the Jews.

The book of Esther relates that, by a decree of the king, the Jews were able to defend themselves on the day their enemies planned to attack them. Here the narrator of the book speaks, describing what happened. Mordecai already had authority, and for that reason the people were not overcome. Some scholars see this as self-defense in the midst of a real threat; others feel uneasy about the number of dead. The text only reports what happened.

For today: God cares for his people in times of danger, but we must take this with seriousness and humility, without seeking revenge. We can trust God and ask him for wisdom to defend what is right without hatred.
exp.4:11:
Haman keeps boasting before his friends and his wife. He says that Queen Esther invited no one but him to the banquet she prepared for the king. He was also invited again for tomorrow.

Haman speaks at home, after leaving the banquet. He has just bragged about his wealth, his sons, and his power. He does this to feel important, but the next verse shows that he is bitter because of Mordecai, who will not bow down to him. What Haman does not know is that Esther is preparing something against him.

For today: let us watch over pride. Haman had honor, money, and family, but he had no peace, because his heart was full of resentment. Let us seek humility and give thanks to God, instead of measuring our worth by the approval of others.
exp.8:31:
This verse says that an order from Queen Esther gave firm support to what had been established about the festival of Purim. It was also recorded in a book. The word "decree" means an authoritative order or command. "Confirmed" means that she gave it validity and backing. "It was written in the book" means it was put in writing, though it is not known with certainty which book is meant.

Here the narrator of the book of Esther is speaking. Mordecai had already sent letters to the Jews throughout the kingdom so that they would observe Purim every year. Now Esther, as queen, supports that decision with her authority. In this way the festival would not be something passing, but a lasting reminder that God took care of his people.

For today: let us not allow the memories of God's faithfulness to fade. Write down the occasions when God helped you, and share them with your family so that you can give thanks together.
exp.1:13:
What it says: Each young woman spent one night with King Ahasuerus. She went in the evening and the next morning returned to another house of the women, called "the second house". There she was kept under Shaashgaz, a eunuch (an official of the court) in charge of the concubines, that is, the king's secondary wives. She no longer came back to the king, unless he took delight in her and had her called by name.

Context: This is the account of the narrator of the book of Esther. It explains how the king sought a new queen after Vashti was removed. The scene shows a harsh court system, where women had very little freedom. It prepares the way for Esther's entrance.

For today: God can work in unjust or painful places, even though he does not approve of them. We can trust that he cares for those who live in situations they did not choose, and we can defend the dignity of vulnerable people.
exp.6:0:
This verse says that King Ahasuerus went with Haman to a banquet to drink wine with Queen Esther. "Came" means that they arrived, and "drink" here refers to a banquet, a dinner with wine.

The narrator is the author of the book of Esther. Esther had already invited the king and Haman to a first banquet, and now the second takes place. She does not yet know how the king will react, but she is preparing to plead for her people, the Jews, whom Haman had condemned to death. This banquet is the key moment when she will speak.

For today: Esther did not rush or act on impulse; she waited for the right moment and prepared herself with courage. When you face a difficult situation, pray, prepare yourself, and seek wisdom before you speak or act. God can use your patience and your courage to help others.
exp.5:0:
That night the king could not sleep. He asked for the book of records, meaning the official register of the events of the kingdom, and it was read aloud to him. The phrase about his sleep leaving him means that he had insomnia.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Esther. Just before this, Haman had prepared a gallows for Mordecai, and the Jews were in danger because of a decree of destruction. The text does not explain why the king could not sleep or why he chose that reading. Many believers see here the hand of God acting without being named, although the book does not say so directly.

For today: God can work in small and unexpected details, such as a sleepless night. Trust that, even when you cannot see what He is doing, He has not forgotten you.
exp.8:25:
This verse explains why the festival is called Purim. The name comes from "Pur," the word for the lot, because Haman cast lots to choose the day to destroy the Jews. The verse of the word "Pur" is set aside here, since the reader's verse does not contain that wording. The verse goes on to say that they established the festival according to what the letter said, what they themselves had seen, and what had come to their knowledge.

The narrator of the book tells how the Jews of Persia decided to remember their deliverance. Mordecai and Esther wrote letters to fix the celebration. What Haman planned as destruction, God turned into rescue, although in Esther the name of God does not appear explicitly.

For today: let us not allow the memory of the times we were delivered to be lost. Recording and telling what we have seen and heard of God's faithfulness strengthens our faith and that of our children.
exp.1:20:
In those days, while Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate, two of the king's officials, Bigthan and Teresh, who guarded the entrance, became angry and plotted to kill King Ahasuerus.

Laying hands on the king meant attacking him to harm him. The officials who served the king in his court were the ones who attended the palace. The king's gate was a place of daily work and public business, and it is thought that Mordecai held some position there, although the text does not state this clearly.

The narrator tells this event briefly. He does not explain why the guards became angry. Mordecai learned of the plan and warned Esther, who told the king. Everything was written down in the records of the kingdom, and later that record will play a great role in the story.

For today: do what is right even when no one notices or thanks you. Mordecai acted with honesty and loyalty, and God was able to use that act at the right time. Serve faithfully today.
exp.8:18:
This verse says that the Jews who lived in villages and towns without walls kept the fourteenth day of the month Adar. For them it was a day of joy, of feasting with food, and of rest. They also sent portions of food to one another. The people of the villages are those who live in the countryside or in small towns, and the towns without walls are settlements that had no protective city walls.

The writer of the book tells how the feast of Purim began. The Jews had defended themselves against those who wanted to destroy them, and God had delivered them. Those in the villages rested on the fourteenth day; those in Susa, the capital, did so on the fifteenth, because they fought one more day there. That is why the dates differ according to the place.

Today we can do something similar: remember with gratitude how God has cared for us and share that joy with others. This week, invite a neighbor or someone who is alone to a meal, or bring them a dish, and tell them something good that God has done for you.
exp.8:6:
This verse begins a list of the names of ten men whom the Jews killed in Susa, the capital. Here appear the first three: Parshandatha, Dalphon, and Aspatha. The word "then" connects this list with the five hundred men already mentioned. The older form of the letters, shown in some printed editions, is not part of the verse as you read it.

The one who narrates is the author of the book of Esther. He tells what happened on the day when the enemies of the Jews intended to attack them, but King Ahasuerus had allowed them to defend themselves. These ten were sons of Haman. The texts do not explain in detail why they are named, though they perhaps show that the event was real and that the danger was brought to an end.

For today: God cares for his people in moments of threat. We can trust that he sees our struggles, and we should seek justice without letting resentment govern us.
exp.0:13:
This verse names seven counselors of King Ahasuerus: Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan. They were princes of Persia and Media. The phrase "which saw the king's face" means they had direct access to him, something reserved for very few. The phrase "which sat the first in the kingdom" indicates that they held the highest positions.

The narrator of the book explains who the counselors were whom the king consulted. Ahasuerus was furious because Queen Vashti had not obeyed his command. Before acting, he consulted these men, who knew the law and the customs. Shortly afterward, Memucan will be the one who speaks.

For today: having wise counselors close at hand is valuable, but they must be chosen well, and one should seek their advice calmly, not in the middle of anger. Facing a difficult decision, it is wise to pray and listen to prudent voices before acting.
exp.8:7:
This verse continues a list of names. Here three of Haman's ten sons appear: Poratha, Adalia, and Aridatha. The archaic accent mark on a letter is simply part of older spelling, so I will leave it out here. In this list, it means that these sons too were killed by the Jews in Susa.

The narrator of the book of Esther recounts what happened on the day Haman had ordered the Jews destroyed. The king allowed them to defend themselves. Haman's ten sons were part of that enemy. The text emphasizes that the Jews did not take the plunder, and this suggests they acted in defense and not out of greed.

For today: when we must defend ourselves or seek justice, let us do so without greed or any desire for gain. And let us trust that God cares for his people, even when the situation is hard and painful.
exp.7:4:
Esther makes her request to the king with great respect. She speaks as the verse does: "If it please the king, and if I have found favour in his sight, and the thing seem right before the king, and I be pleasing in his eyes." She asks that the letters Haman, the son of Hammedatha, had written to destroy the Jews in all the provinces be reversed.

Queen Esther is the one speaking. Haman had already been hanged, but his decree was still in force, and Persian laws could not easily be cancelled. That is why she comes back, weeping, to plead for her people. The king extends the golden sceptre to show that she may speak.

For today: when someone suffers injustice, it is not enough to be glad that the guilty party has fallen. Esther kept pressing her case with humility, courage and love for her people. We can use whatever voice, influence or prayer we have to stand up for others, trusting that God also works through people who are willing.
exp.5:12:
Haman told his wife Zeresh and all his friends everything that had happened to him: he had been made to honor Mordecai in public. His advisers and Zeresh answered him that, if Mordecai is of the seed of the Jews, Haman will not prevail against him, but will surely fall before him.

Haman was humbled, since the king had ordered him to honor his enemy. His advisers and his wife now speak, the same people who had encouraged his pride before. Now they see that something greater is at work. The text does not explain why they think this way; it only shows their fear before the Jewish people. Soon after, Haman is called to Esther's banquet.

Today we can remember that pride and resentment blind us and in the end bring us down. God can change circumstances, and our plans do not control them. It is better to humble ourselves, ask forgiveness, and trust in Him than to struggle against what He is sustaining.
exp.7:7:
Here the king Ahasuerus gives Esther and Mordecai permission to write a new order in favor of the Jews, using the king's authority. The king's ring served as the official seal. An order sealed in this way cannot be revoked: it could not be cancelled.

The king speaks after Haman, the enemy of the Jews, has been executed. Haman had obtained a decree to destroy the Jewish people, and that law could not be cancelled. For this reason the king allows a second order that gives them protection. Esther had pleaded for her people, and Mordecai now receives authority to act.

For today: when you face a problem that seems to have no way out, pray with courage and seek wise solutions. God can open paths you had not imagined.
exp.0:2:
In the third year of his reign, King Ahasuerus gave a great feast for all his princes and servants. The military leaders of Persia and Media were present, along with the governors and princes of the provinces. "Gave a feast" means that he offered a grand celebration. "The power of Persia and Media" refers to his leaders and army commanders.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, presenting King Ahasuerus (often identified with Xerxes I, though this is a common identification, not a certain one). He gathered his leaders to display the splendor of his power, as the following verses describe. The account sets the stage for the scene in which Esther will appear.

For today: it is easy to impress others with what we have or accomplish. But human power passes away. We can ask ourselves whether we seek our own glory or whether we use what God has given us to serve and honor Him.
exp.4:4:
Here the king responds at once to Esther's invitation. He tells his servants to hurry, and to call Haman so that he may do what the queen asked. Then the king and Haman go to the banquet that Esther prepared.

The one speaking is King Ahasuerus. Esther had come before him without being called, something that could have cost her her life, but he received her with favor. She did not state her real request right away; first she invited the king and Haman, the enemy of her people. Interpreters often see here Esther's wisdom and patience, although the text does not explain all of her motives.

For today: when we face a difficult situation, we can pray and act with wisdom and patience, without rushing ahead, trusting that God can prepare the right moment.
exp.0:19:
It says that when the king publishes his decree, it will be known throughout his vast kingdom. According to the adviser, all the women, from the most important to the most humble, would then show respect to their husbands. "They will give honor" means to respect or hold in high regard. "For it is great" refers to how wide the empire is.

The one speaking is Memucan, one of the princes of King Ahasuerus. Queen Vashti had refused to appear before the king at a banquet, and Memucan feared that other women would follow her example. His proposal comes from fear and wounded pride, and the text only reports that the king accepted it, not that God approved it.

For today: true respect is not achieved through orders or fear. It is earned through love, humility, and good treatment. As Ephesians 5:21 says, the Bible invites us to submit to one another out of reverence for Christ.
exp.8:8:
This verse continues the list of the ten sons of Haman. Here the names given are Parmashta, Arisai, Aridai and Vajezatha. The sentence about the old spelling of the letter "á" is removed, since the reader's verse has no such spelling. The names are Persian names.

The narrator of the book of Esther tells what happened when Haman wanted to destroy the Jews. The king allowed them to defend themselves. That defense included Haman's sons, who were part of the threat. The text repeats that they did not take the plunder, and this shows that they did not act for gain. Some scholars think the very detailed list emphasizes that the event was real and official.

For today: when you have to defend what is right, do it with a clean heart. Do not use conflicts to gain personal advantage. Ask God to keep you from greed.
exp.4:3:
Esther answers the king respectfully. She asks him to come today, together with Haman, to a banquet she has prepared. The phrase "if it seem good unto the king" is an old way of saying "if it pleases the king." The word "seem" here means to appear or to be pleasing.

Esther has just come before the king without having been called, which could have cost her her life. The king shows her favor and even offers her up to half the kingdom. She does not yet ask for what she truly needs, which is to save her people. Instead, she prefers to invite him to a banquet. The Bible does not explain why, but many believe she was waiting for the right moment and acting with caution.

Today we can learn that it is not always wise to rush. Before speaking or acting in difficult situations, it is good to pray, think calmly, and ask God for wisdom to choose the right moment.
exp.6:9:
This verse tells us that Haman was hanged on the very gallows he had set up to kill Mordecai. "Prepared" here means set up or arranged, and the "gallows" was a tall wooden post on which a person was put to death. When this happened, the king's anger was calmed.

The narrator sums up the end of Haman's fall. He had planned to destroy Mordecai and the whole Jewish people. But Queen Esther revealed his plan to King Ahasuerus, and the king, furious, ordered that Haman be hanged. Some see in this an ironic justice; the book does not name God, but it shows how the evil planned against others turns back on the one who devised it.

For today: we do not have to take revenge or live in bitterness when someone wrongs us. We can act with courage and truth, as Esther did, and trust that God knows how to bring about justice in his time (Romans 12:19).
exp.5:13:
While they were still speaking with him, the king's officials arrived and hurried to bring Haman to the banquet that Esther had prepared. The word "prepared" here means arranged or made ready.

Haman had just been humiliated: he had to publicly honor Mordecai, whom he hated. His advisers had warned him that if Mordecai was Jewish, he would not defeat him. He was given no time to think, for he was taken right away to Esther's second banquet, where she would reveal her plan. The account does not mention God, but it shows how everything falls into place at the right time.

For today: even when evil plans seem to be moving forward, God can work in the details and the timing. We can trust in his justice, without seeking revenge or despairing.
exp.3:10:
Esther sent word back to Mordecai that everyone in the kingdom knows a very harsh rule: whoever enters the king's inner court without being summoned must die. The only exception is that the king extends his golden scepter toward that person, and then they live. The scepter is the rod that symbolizes the king's authority. Esther adds that for thirty days the king has not called for her.

Queen Esther is speaking, answering through the messenger Hatach. Mordecai had asked her to plead with the king to save the Jews from the decree of destruction. She explains the real danger that doing so would involve. It is not a clear refusal; it shows her fear and her limits.

For today: when God calls us to do something difficult, we can be honest about our fears, as Esther was. Saying "I am afraid" is not a lack of faith. What matters is not to stop there, but to seek the counsel of other believers and ask God for courage.
exp.8:2:
This verse says that all the officials of the Persian empire, that is, the governors of the provinces, the viceroys, the captains and the king's officers, supported and favored the Jews. The reason is that the fear of Mordecai, that is, the respect and dread of his power, had fallen upon them.

Here the narrator of the book of Esther is speaking. The 13th day of Adar was the date set for attacking the Jews, but the situation was turned around. Mordecai was already very important at the court of King Ahasuerus, and that is why the officials sided with the Jews.

For today: God can change situations that seem lost, often in unexpected ways. Trust Him when everything seems against you, and humbly use whatever influence He gives you to protect others.
exp.1:16:
This verse tells that King Ahasuerus chose Esther from among all the young women who were presented to him. He loved her more than the others, and she won his favour and approval. So he set the royal crown on her head and made her queen instead of Vashti. Words such as "grace and favour" mean kindness, acceptance and goodwill.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, relating the events. Vashti had been removed from her place as queen, and the king was seeking to replace her. Esther, a young Jewish woman raised by her cousin Mordecai, was brought into the palace. She followed the advice of Hegai, the keeper of the women. The text does not mention God, but many readers see his care working quietly.

For today: Even when we do not see God working in an obvious way, we can trust that he cares for our lives. In the meantime, let us live with humility, attentive to good counsel and willing to serve wherever he places us.
exp.1:8:
Hegai, the official in charge of the women, liked Esther and she won his favor. So he quickly gave her her beauty supplies and her special food, and assigned her seven chosen maidens from the palace. He also moved her and her maids to the best place in the women's quarters. Here "beauty supplies" refers to the personal items used for adornment and care of appearance, and "quickly" means without delay.

This is part of the account in which the king seeks a new queen and gathers many young women in Susa. Esther, an orphan raised by her cousin Mordecai, is brought into the palace. The narrator reports the events without speaking of God directly; many readers see his care behind these happenings, though the text does not say so.

For today: even in foreign or difficult places, God can give us unexpected favor and support. Live with integrity and gratitude, and trust that He works even when we cannot clearly see it.
exp.8:23:
This verse explains why the feast of Purim exists. Haman, a descendant of Agag, saw the Jews as enemies and planned to destroy them completely. He cast the lot, a way of deciding something by chance, like rolling dice or drawing lots, to choose the day for his plan.

The narrator of the book of Esther summarizes what happened here, to explain the name of the feast. The Jews had gone from sorrow to joy, and Mordecai asked them to remember that deliverance with feasts, gifts, and help for the poor.

For today: Haman believed that chance would decide the fate of a people, but the outcome was different. We can trust that God cares for his people even when everything seems uncertain. And when we receive relief, let us do as they did: give thanks and share with those in need.
exp.3:4:
This verse tells how Esther, the queen, called Hatach, one of the king's chamberlains, meaning an official of the court whom the king had assigned to attend her. She sent him to Mordecai to find out what was wrong and why he was in such a state. The verse's note on the wording is dropped here, since "to find out" and "to know what it was, and why it was" carry the same sense in the verse your reader sees.

The narrator then describes how Esther reacts on seeing her cousin Mordecai's grief. He was wearing mourning clothes because the king had decreed the destruction of the Jews. Esther felt distress, but she did not yet know the reason. So she sends someone she trusts to ask, rather than assuming.

When someone suffers near us, it is not enough to feel sorry or to send a gift. It is wise to draw close, ask with kindness, and listen to the whole story before acting.
exp.4:13:
This verse tells how Zeresh, Haman's wife, and his friends advise him to build a gallows, very tall, fifty cubits high (about 22 meters, roughly). They suggest he ask the king to hang Mordecai on it, and then go cheerfully to the banquet. The word "pleased" in the verse means that Haman liked the idea, and he ordered the gallows to be prepared.

Haman has just boasted of his wealth and honor, but he admits that all of it means nothing to him as long as Mordecai does not bow before him. His wounded pride has turned into hatred. Those around him, instead of calming him, feed his resentment. What Haman does not know is that this gallows will become his own end, as the book will show later.

Today, stored-up resentment can grow until it controls us. Let us ask God for humility and seek counselors who bring us toward peace, not those who stir up our anger. As Proverbs 16:18 says, pride comes before destruction.
exp.3:15:
Esther asks Mordecai to gather all the Jews of Shushan and fast for her for three days, neither eating nor drinking, day or night. She and her maidens will fast the same way. Afterward she will go in before the king, even though the law does not allow it. She says, "if I perish, I perish," meaning she accepts the risk of dying.

Esther speaks from the palace in Persia. Mordecai had told her not to keep silent, because the Jewish people were threatened with destruction. Going in without being called could cost her her life. The text does not mention God, but the fasting suggests they were seeking help beyond what was human.

For today: before a difficult decision, do not act alone or in a rush. Ask others to pray with you, seek God with humility, and then take the right step, even when it costs you.
exp.2:13:
This verse says that a copy of the king's decree was published in every province and to all peoples. In this way, everyone would know that they must be ready, or prepared and informed, for that appointed day.

The narrator of the book tells how Haman, a high official, managed to get King Ahasuerus to sign an order to destroy the Jews on the thirteenth day of Adar. The decree was translated into every language and spread so that no one could ignore it. Meanwhile, the king and Haman sat down calmly to drink, but the city of Susa was bewildered and distressed.

For today: evil sometimes seems to advance with order and power, but God does not lose control. When you face injustice or fear, pray, seek wise counsel, and do not remain silent or alone. God can work even when it is not yet visible.
exp.4:10:
Here Haman gathers his friends and his wife Zeresh, and begins to boast. He tells them of his great riches, his many sons, and all the honors the king had given him. In the verse, the phrase "promoted him" and the phrase "advanced him above the princes" describe how the king raised him up and placed him above the other officials of the kingdom and above the king's servants.

Haman had just left Queen Esther's banquet happy, but he was filled with rage when he saw that Mordecai would not bow down before him. At home, he looks for applause to soothe his wounded pride. The next verse shows that, even with so much glory, he could not be at peace.

For today: riches, fame, and achievements do not fill the heart. If we depend on the approval of others, any slight will take away our peace. Let us seek our worth in God, who gives humility and rest.
exp.0:5:
This verse describes how the place of the king's feast was decorated. There were hangings of white, green, and dark blue, fastened with cords of fine linen and purple to silver rings and marble pillars. The couches, that is, the couches on which the guests reclined, were of gold and silver. The floor was a mosaic of precious stones, such as porphyry, marble, and alabaster.

The narrator of the book tells this to show the enormous wealth of King Ahasuerus (Xerxes) in his palace at Susa. The banquets were meant to display his power before nobles and people. Here it sets the scene for the events that follow in the story.

For today: human beauty and luxury impress us, but they pass away. We can enjoy what God gives us without placing our security in it, and remember that He works even behind scenes of great power.
exp.3:7:
Here Mordecai hands Hathach a written copy of the decree that was published in Shushan to destroy the Jews. Hathach was to show it to Esther and explain everything to her. In addition, Mordecai charges her to go before the king, make her plea to him, and ask on behalf of her people.

Hathach is a servant of the king, sent by Esther. Mordecai, her cousin and guardian, is in mourning over Haman's decree. He wants Esther to see the proof in writing and understand that the danger is real. As queen, she had access to the king, although approaching him without being called was risky.

For today: when you come across an injustice or a need, do not stay silent or occupied only with your own affairs. Ask whether God has placed you where you can speak, pray, or help, and take the first step with humility.
exp.7:6:
Here the king Ahasuerus reminds Queen Esther and Mordecai the Jew of what he has already done for them: he gave Esther the house of Haman, and Haman was hanged on the gallows because he set out to attack the Jews.

The king is speaking in response to Esther's plea, since she had just begged him with tears to overturn Haman's decree ordering the destruction of all the Jews. The king points to what has already been done, and in the verses that follow he gives them permission to write a new decree. Persian law could not be revoked, so another way out was sought.

For today: when an injustice threatens others, Esther teaches us not to stay silent. We can use with courage and respect whatever influence we have, whether little or much, to defend those who are in danger.
exp.6:5:
Here Esther clearly identifies the guilty party: the enemy and adversary is Haman. "Adversary" means someone who opposes others and seeks to do them harm. "Was afraid" means he was overcome with terror and dread, and did not know what to do before the king and the queen.

Esther speaks at the banquet she prepared for King Ahasuerus. Up to that moment he did not know that she was a Jew, nor that her people were condemned by a decree that Haman had promoted. After praying and preparing herself, Esther finally reveals the truth and asks for justice, risking her own life.

For today: sometimes we must speak with courage and truth in the face of injustice, even when it is frightening. We can do so with respect and prudence, trusting that God cares for his people and can use our voice at the right moment.
exp.7:14:
This verse tells how Mordecai came out from the presence of King Ahasuerus dressed like someone of high rank. He wore clothing of blue and white, a great golden crown, and a garment of fine linen and purple. The whole city of Shushan filled with joy.

The narrator describes the change in the situation. Earlier, Haman had obtained a decree to destroy the Jews. Now Haman is gone, and the king honors Mordecai, who had been loyal. A new decree allowed the Jews to defend themselves. That is why the city celebrates.

For today: even when injustice seems to win, God can change situations in his own time. We can keep acting with faithfulness and hope, and rejoice when justice makes its way.
exp.7:12:
This verse says that a copy of the king's decree was to be published in every province, so that all peoples would know it. The message was that the Jews were to be ready for that day. They could defend themselves and act against those who attacked them.

King Ahasuerus, through Mordecai and Esther, responds to the earlier decree of Haman, which ordered the destruction of the Jews. Because a Persian law could not be revoked, another was issued that allowed them to defend themselves. The text presents it as a defense of the people's lives. Some readers notice that the language is harsh, and that is understandable within its time and its situation of danger.

For today: when you face a threat or an injustice, do not remain passive, nor act out of hatred. Seek with wisdom the just ways to protect those who depend on you, and trust that God cares for his own.
exp.7:11:
This verse gives the date on which the Jews could defend themselves: one single day in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is the month Adar. King Ahasuerus is the Persian king known as Xerxes. Adar was the last month of the Hebrew calendar, falling between February and March.

Mordecai writes in the king's name and seals the letter with the king's signet. Earlier, Haman had obtained a decree to destroy the Jews on that very day, and a decree of the king could not be revoked. So a new decree is issued that allows them to defend their lives. Some readers see in the words about children and women a reply to the first decree; others debate how they should be understood.

God cared for his people even though his name does not appear in the book. Today we can trust that he works in difficult circumstances, even when we do not see him. In the meantime, let us act with courage and wisdom, and do what is within our reach.
exp.0:10:
What it says: King Ahasuerus, merry with wine, orders that Queen Vashti be brought before him wearing the royal crown. He wants to display her beauty before the peoples and the princes, because she was lovely to look on.

Context: The speaker is the king, on the seventh day of a great feast. Vashti was holding a separate feast of her own, for the women. He gives the order through seven eunuchs, or court officials. The text does not say exactly how she was supposed to appear, and some think it meant only with the crown, though this is an interpretation. What is clear is that he treated her as something to be shown off.

For today: People are worth more than their appearance or what they add to our image. Let us ask God for a heart that respects others, especially when we have power and decisions are made with a clouded mind.
exp.8:28:
This verse says that Queen Esther, daughter of Abihail, and Mordecai the Jew wrote with full authority a second letter to establish the feast of Purim. The phrase "with all authority" means with firmness and with authority, and the word "establish" means to make something well settled.

The book of Esther tells how God rescued the Jews from Haman's plan to destroy them. After that victory, Esther and Mordecai wanted the people never to forget what had happened. For that reason they put the yearly celebration in writing and sent it to all the provinces. Although God's name does not appear in this book, many see Him acting behind the events.

For today: remembering what God has done for us is important. We can write down or tell about the times God helped us, to thank Him and to encourage our family to trust Him.
exp.7:13:
The messengers of the king went out very quickly to carry the new law. They rode on camels and mules, which were beasts used for carrying loads and for travel. The word "hastened" means that they were pressed on by the urgency of the order. "Shushan" is Susa, the capital. The law was given there, and from there it went out to the whole kingdom.

The one who tells the story is the author of the book of Esther. Earlier, Haman had obtained a decree to destroy the Jews, and a decree of the king could not be revoked. So Ahasuerus, at the request of Esther and Mordecai, authorized another decree that allowed the Jews to defend themselves. There was little time, and that is why there was such haste.

For today: when you have good news or help that others need, do not put it off. A word of encouragement, a piece of advice, or a prayer offered in time can ease someone who lives with fear.
exp.1:0:
Esther 2:1 says that after these things, when the anger of King Ahasuerus had calmed down, he remembered Vashti, what she had done, and what had been decreed against her. The word "calmed" here means that his anger had settled. The phrase "what had been decreed against her" refers to the order to remove her from her place as queen.

Context: the narrator of the book tells what happened in the palace of Persia. In chapter 1, Vashti refused to come before the king, and he, angry, removed her from her position. Here the text does not say whether he felt sadness, regret, or simply remembered. His servants notice his mood and propose that they search for a new queen.

For today: decisions made in anger often bring consequences that we later regret. Before acting while angry, it is wise to wait, pray, and think calmly. God can also work in the middle of difficult situations, even when we cannot yet see it.
exp.5:9:
Here the king Ahasuerus orders Haman to carry out at once what Haman himself proposed: take the royal robe and the horse, and honor Mordecai the Jew, who sits at the king's gate.

The king speaks to Haman, who believed the honor would be for himself, and so had described a great distinction. Ahasuerus did not know that Haman hated Mordecai. Shortly before, the king had remembered that Mordecai had never been rewarded for saving his life. Thus Haman is bound to honor his enemy.

For today: it is not worth living to seek applause or to hold on to resentment. Pride can lead us to shame, while God cares for the humble and works even when we do not see it. We can serve faithfully and trust that He knows how to act in His own time.
exp.7:9:
He wrote letters in the name of King Ahasuerus and sealed them with the royal signet ring, which served as the official signature. He sent them by couriers on horseback, riding on mules, camels, and swift young dromedaries, meaning fast animals used in the king's service.

After Haman had plotted to destroy the Jews, the king's first decree could not be revoked. So Esther and Mordecai received permission to write a second decree. This one did not cancel the first, but it allowed the Jews to defend themselves. The text emphasizes urgency: word had to reach every province quickly.

For today: when there is an urgent need, God often uses ordinary means, such as planning, communication, and diligent effort. We can pray in faith and also act wisely to help others in time.
exp.1:14:
This verse tells us that the turn came for Esther to present herself before the king. She was the daughter of Abihail, the uncle of Mordecai, who had taken her in and raised her as his own daughter. Esther did not ask for anything special; she simply accepted what Hegai, the chamberlain in charge of the women, advised her. And everyone who saw her came to think well of her.

It is the narrator of the book who speaks. Esther is in the palace of King Ahasuerus, within a long process of choosing a new queen. Other young women asked for ornaments and things to make a good impression, but she acted with simplicity and trust in the advice of someone who knew how the process worked. The book does not explain why she pleased everyone; it simply presents it.

For today: it is not always necessary to appear more than others. Humility, knowing how to listen, and accepting good advice can open doors and leave a good impression without forcing anything.
exp.8:30:
This verse says that the days of Purim were to be kept each year on their appointed dates. Mordecai and Queen Esther had commanded it, and the people accepted it for themselves and for their children. "Seed" means descendants. The feast would remind them of the end of the fasts and the cry, that is, the time of distress and prayer.

The narrator of the book tells how Mordecai and Esther wrote a second letter to the Jews in the one hundred and twenty-seven provinces of the kingdom. They wanted Purim to be firmly established as a lasting custom. The Jews had been saved from a plan to destroy them, and this feast would keep that memory alive. The text gives no further details about how the fasting was done, only that it would be remembered.

For today: when God delivers us from a difficulty, it is good to remember it on purpose. We can write a prayer of thanksgiving, tell our children what God did, or set aside a day to give thanks. In this way faith passes from one generation to the next.
exp.1:11:
This verse tells us that each young woman had to spend twelve months in preparation before she could be presented to King Ahasuerus. For six months they used oil of myrrh, a fragrant oil, and for the other six months they used sweet odours and other things for purifying and beautifying. The young women are the maids, and the preparation itself is the beautifying process.

It is the narrator of the book who explains the custom of the Persian court. After Ahasuerus put Queen Vashti away, they gathered many young women so that another queen could be chosen. Mordecai, Esther's cousin and guardian, watched from a distance over how she was doing, and he had asked her not to reveal her Jewish origin. The text gives no further details about the process.

For today: God works within long processes and situations we did not choose. Esther waited, and later her position would help save her people. We can trust that God uses our times of waiting, even when we cannot yet see the purpose.
exp.0:16:
It says that what Queen Vashti did would become known among all the women of the kingdom. According to the counselor, they would begin to look with little respect on their husbands, saying: "The king commanded Vashti to be brought in, and she did not come."

The speaker is Memucan, one of the princes of King Ahasuerus. Vashti had refused to appear before the king and his guests during a great feast. Memucan turns a personal matter into a danger for the whole kingdom. Some think he was exaggerating to flatter the king and to protect the men in power. Here the Bible simply recounts what happened without necessarily approving his advice.

For today: before reacting with anger or fear, it is wise to pause and think. The advice of those who seek their own benefit may sound wise, but it is not always just. Let us ask God for humility and good judgment.
exp.1:12:
When it was each young woman's turn to go in to the king, she could ask for whatever she wanted to take with her. Everything was given to her. The verse also explains that a young woman is a maiden, and that the place in the palace where they were prepared was the house of the women.

It is the narrator of the book who describes the process of choosing the new queen, after Vashti was removed. The young women spent a year in preparation. The text does not explain what they asked for or why; we do not know for certain. Later on it becomes clear that Esther asked for nothing, but followed the advice of Hegai, and won the favor of everyone.

For today: we do not always win by having more, but by having a simple and humble heart. We can ask ourselves whether we are seeking to impress others, or whether we trust the guidance of wise people while God works quietly.
exp.1:15:
This verse tells that Esther was taken to the royal palace of King Ahasuerus, that is, Xerxes in other versions. It happened in the tenth month, called Tebeth, which roughly corresponds to December or January, in the seventh year of his reign.

It is the narrator of the book who speaks, and he gives precise dates to place the event. Esther had already gone through a period of preparation with the other young women. Earlier it is said that she won the favor of everyone who saw her and that she followed only what Hegai advised her. This moment leads to the next verse: the king makes her queen.

For today: Esther did not rush or seek to impose herself; she acted with humility and patience. We can trust that God works in times that seem slow, and meanwhile live with simplicity and good character.
exp.5:11:
After honoring Mordecai through the streets, Mordecai returned to his duties at the king's gate. Haman, on the other hand, ran home full of sorrow and with his head covered.

The narrator recounts this unexpected turn. Haman had planned to hang Mordecai, but the king asked him to publicly honor his enemy. Mordecai is not puffed up by the honor; he remains in his place of service. Haman, humiliated, seeks comfort from his family, who warn him that he is headed for a fall.

For today: when you receive recognition, or when someone else receives it and it hurts you, remember that pride sinks us and humility keeps us steady. God is the one who lifts up and who brings low. Keep doing your duty with simplicity and trust that he cares for your cause.
exp.8:14:
The verse says that the Jews in Shushan gathered together on the fourteenth day of the month of Adar and killed three hundred men. Even so, they did not take anything of the spoil. The verse of "spoil" and "laid not their hand" has been omitted here, since the reader's verse uses the phrase "on the prey they laid not their hand" and the sentence is about what they did not take.

It is part of the story of Esther. A decree allowed the Jews to defend themselves against those who wanted to destroy them. Esther asked the king for one more day in Shushan, and the king granted it. The text stresses that they did not plunder, to show that they were acting in defense and not out of greed. Some readers see this as a contrast with Haman's original decree, which ordered that everything be taken from them.

For today: when you have to defend what is right, do so with limits and without seeking personal gain. Let your motives be clean, and let neither anger nor self-interest lead you to take advantage of anyone.
exp.3:16:
It says that Mordecai went his way and did all that Esther had asked of him. The phrase "went his way" means "went his way" in plain terms, and the phrase "did according to all" is rendered here as "did all according to." In other words, Mordecai obeyed Esther's instructions without arguing.

The narrator tells what happened after Esther's message. The Jewish people were in danger because of a decree of death. Esther decided to approach the king without being summoned, which could cost her her life. She asked that all the Jews in Susa fast with her for three days. Mordecai, who had once given orders to her, now obeys her. This shows a change of roles and his trust in her.

For today: when someone takes a brave step and asks for support, let us help with humility. Sometimes God calls us to follow others, even though we may once have been the ones leading. Let us pray and walk alongside them in faith.
exp.1:2:
This verse is part of the advice that the king's servants give to Ahasuerus. They propose that the king appoint officers in all the provinces to gather the young virgins of fair appearance, that is, of beautiful look. They would be brought to Shushan, the city where the king resided, to the house of the women. There they would be placed under the care of Hegai, a eunuch (a court official) in charge of the women. They would also be given what was needed for their personal preparation.

The servants speak after the king's anger against Vashti, who had been removed, had calmed down. They seek to replace her and, at the same time, to please the king. This was a custom of the Persian court; the text describes it, but it does not say that God approves of it.

For today: God can work even in unjust or cold environments, without everything that happens being good. Trust that he cares for his people, even when we do not yet see how.
exp.8:21:
This verse explains what was to be remembered in those days: the time when the Jews rested from their enemies, and the month when their sorrow was turned into joy and their mourning into a good day. Because of this, they were to make those days times of feasting and gladness. They were also to send portions of food to one another, and to give gifts to the poor.

Mordecai, a Jew who became very important in the kingdom of Ahasuerus, writes this letter to the Jews in all the provinces. Their deliverance had just happened: Haman had planned to destroy them, but that plan failed. Mordecai wants them not to forget what happened and to celebrate it every year. This is the story of the feast of Purim.

For today: when God delivers us from something difficult, it is good to remember it with gratitude. But it is not celebrated alone: it is shared with neighbors, and help is given to those in need.
exp.8:27:
This verse says that the days of Purim were to be remembered and observed everywhere: in every nation, family, province, and city. The phrase "should not fail from among the Jews" means they would never disappear from among them. "Seed" means descendants, that is, children and grandchildren. The idea is that each generation would keep the memory alive.

The story of Esther tells how the Jewish people in the Persian empire were saved from a plan to destroy them. Here the author explains how the Jews, together with Esther and Mordecai, established a yearly feast to remember that deliverance. Purim comes from "Pur," the lot that was cast to set the date of the attack.

For today: do not let God's kindnesses be forgotten. You can write down or tell within your family how God helped you in difficult moments, so that younger ones learn to trust him.
exp.2:2:
The king's servants who guarded the palace gate asked Mordecai why he was disobeying the king's order. "Transgress" means to go beyond or over something, that is, to disobey or break a command.

These are the officials who worked at the king's gate, where Mordecai also served. The king had ordered everyone to bow down before Haman, but Mordecai did not do so. The text does not explain his reason here; it only says later that he had told them he was a Jew. Some think he acted for religious reasons, others because of the hostility between his people and the Agagites, and the Bible does not make this clear in this passage.

Some convictions bring pressure, and at times others do not understand our firmness. Let us ask God for wisdom to remain faithful with humility and courage, trusting that he cares for us even when it costs us.
exp.5:6:
Haman answers King Ahasuerus with the very words the king used to ask him: "For the man whom the king delighteth to honour". This is the opening of his reply, which continues in the verses that follow. Here "man" simply means a man, and "honour" refers to public recognition.

Haman is a high official of the kingdom. The king asks him how to honour someone, but does not say who. Haman, thinking it must be himself, says to himself: "Whom would the king desire to honour more than me?" That is why he asks for very great honours. In truth, the king wanted to honour Mordecai, the Jew whom Haman hated.

For today: pride leads us to assume things and to seek the first places. Let us rather learn to serve with humility and let God, in his time, be the one who honours us, as Proverbs 27:2 says.
exp.1:17:
Then the king Ahasuerus made a great feast for all his princes and servants, and he called it "Esther's feast." He also gave relief to the provinces, which may mean he lifted taxes or gave the people a rest from burdens, though the text gives no exact details. He distributed gifts with the generosity fitting a king.

No one speaks here; the narrator is telling the story. Esther has just been crowned queen in place of Vashti. The king celebrates with a public feast and gestures of kindness toward the people. What the book does not yet say is how God will use this place of Esther's later on, since God's name does not appear in the book at all.

For today: when we receive a blessing or a new position, we can use it to benefit others, not only to enjoy it. And we can trust that God works even in what seems ordinary and everyday.
exp.5:1:
Here it is told that, when reading the records of the kingdom, the king found a fact written down: Mordecai had reported a plot. Two eunuchs, Bigthana and Teresh, the guards of the palace door, wanted to lay hand on the king, that is, to attack him to harm him. "Reported" means that he informed the authorities.

The narrator of the book connects the events. The king could not sleep and asked for the chronicles to be read to him. That reading led him right to this forgotten episode, which is mentioned earlier in Esther 2. Mordecai was never rewarded. The text does not name God, but many readers see here his discreet care, since everything happens just before Haman asks for Mordecai's death.

For today: do good even when no one thanks you. God sees what others forget, and he can give its right moment to what you did faithfully.
exp.8:12:
Esther asks the king for two things: that the Jews in Shushan may defend themselves one more day, just as they did the day before, and that the bodies of Haman's ten sons be hanged on the gallows. "Shushan" is the capital city, and the word for "pleasing" means "if it seems good to the king." Hanging them probably refers to displaying their bodies after they were already dead, though some understand it in another way.

Queen Esther is speaking. King Ahasuerus has just told her about the five hundred dead in Shushan, and he offers to grant her another request. Haman had planned to destroy the Jews, and the decree could not be cancelled, so they had permission to defend themselves. Esther asks for more time, probably because enemies were still in the city.

For today: Esther used her position with courage to protect her people. You too can use your influence to defend the vulnerable, but this scene is a historical account, not a model of revenge. Jesus calls us to love even our enemies.
exp.2:10:
Here the king Ahasuerus answers Haman. Some interpret that the king refuses the money as a gesture of courtesy, while others hold that he simply hands it over; the text does not make this clear.

The speaker is King Ahasuerus, who does not know that Esther is a Jew. Haman, angry at Mordecai, had presented the Jews as a dangerous people. The king gives him his ring, which served as the official seal, and so Haman gains the authority to issue a decree of destruction.

Today this reminds us that power used without asking questions or investigating can cause enormous harm. Before repeating accusations against others, or making decisions that affect them, let us seek the truth and think about their dignity as people created by God.
exp.8:19:
Esther 9:20 says that Mordecai wrote down what had happened and sent letters to all the Jews of the kingdom of King Ahasuerus. He did this both to those who lived nearby and to those who lived far away.

The narrator of the book tells how the Jews had been spared from a plan to destroy them. Mordecai, who had risen to a position of influence, wanted no one to forget that deliverance. So he wrote, and in the verses that follow he asks that each year it be celebrated with a feast, joy, gifts to neighbors, and help for the poor.

For today: do not keep silent about what God has done for you. Write it down, share it with others, and let it become gratitude and generosity toward those who most need it.
exp.0:21:
Esther 1:22 tells us that King Ahasuerus sent letters to all the provinces of his kingdom. Each one was written in the script and language of its own people. The decree said that every man should be the master in his own home, that is, rule over his household. "Pleased" is the word here for "agreed with" or "delighted," and "letters" means written messages or documents.

After Queen Vashti refused to appear before the king at a banquet, Memucan, one of his counselors, feared that other wives would do the same. The king followed his advice and issued this decree. The book only reports the event and does not approve of it. Many readers see in the scene the pride and insecurity of the Persian court.

Today we can notice that ruling the home by decree does not produce true respect. The Bible teaches that the home is built up with love, humility, and mutual service (Ephesians 5:21). Let us ask God for wisdom to treat our family with respect.
exp.2:14:
The posts went out quickly, by the king's order, to carry the decree against the Jews. The edict was also published in Susa, the capital. "Quickly" means in a hurry. "Perplexed" means troubled and confused. Meanwhile, the king and Haman sat down to drink, and the city was distressed.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Haman, a high official, had managed to get the king to sign a decree to destroy the Jews, out of his hatred for Mordecai. The contrast is strong: two men drink together calmly, while ordinary people are filled with fear at such injustice.

For today: do not be indifferent to the pain of others. Even when others live at ease, you can care about those who suffer, pray for them, and help in whatever way you can. God sees what seems hidden.
exp.0:4:
When these days were ended, the king gave another feast, this time lasting seven days. It was held in the court of the garden, that is, the garden of the palace. He invited all the people who were present in Shushan the capital, "both great and small," that is, from the most important to the most humble.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Esther. He tells the events concerning King Ahasuerus (also called Xerxes in other translations, although some scholars debate the identification). His purpose is to show the enormous wealth and power of the king, and to set the stage for the appearance of Esther later on.

For today: luxury and human power impress, but they do not last. We can enjoy what God gives us with gratitude, without placing our security in it, but in Him, who governs even behind the scenes.
