exp.7:8:
On the twenty-third day of Sivan, the third month, which falls roughly between May and June, the king's secretaries were summoned. There they wrote down everything Mordecai commanded, and the letters were addressed to the Jews and to the officials: the satraps (governors), the captains and the princes of the 127 provinces, from India to Ethiopia. Each letter was written in the language and script of its own people, and also in that of the Jews.

Background: Haman had obtained a decree to destroy the Jews, and that law could not be revoked. So King Ahasuerus gave Esther and Mordecai permission to write a second decree that would allow the Jews to defend themselves.

For today: For a message to reach the heart, it has to be communicated in a way people can understand. Think about how you can explain your faith in simple, close words, without assuming that everyone understands your language.
exp.6:7:
King Ahasuerus returned from the palace garden to the room where the banquet was held. There he found Haman thrown down on the couch where Queen Esther was reclining. The phrase "to force" here means to assault or to do violence. The king asked whether Haman would dare to do such a thing inside his own house. Covering Haman's face was a sign of condemnation: Haman was now sentenced.

Esther had just accused Haman of being the enemy of her people. The king left in anger, and Haman stayed behind begging for his life. When he fell onto the couch, he was probably trying to plead for mercy, but the king saw it differently. Interpreters agree that Haman did not intend to attack her, though the king took it that way.

For today: pride and wickedness may seem powerful, but sooner or later they are exposed. We can trust that God is at work even when we cannot see it, and act with courage and truth, as Esther did.
exp.8:13:
This verse says that King Ahasuerus approved what Esther asked for. The order was published in the capital, and Haman's ten sons were hanged. "Shushan" is the city of Susa, and "hanged" means their bodies were put on display on the gallows, probably after they had died, though the text does not make this clear.

Esther speaks with the king after the first day of fighting, when the Jews defended themselves against Haman's decree that sought their destruction. She asks for one more day and for the public display of Haman's sons. Some believe this was a signal meant to discourage other enemies; the text does not explain more. Note that the Jews did not take any plunder.

For today: this passage reminds us that unjust evil has consequences, but it also invites us to seek justice without greed or personal revenge. Let us trust that God cares for his people, and ask him for wisdom to act with righteousness.
exp.6:3:
Here Esther says that she and her people have been "sold," that is, handed over to their enemies, to be destroyed, killed, and exterminated. She says that if they had only been sold as male and female servants, she would have kept silent. The last sentence is difficult: it seems to say that this lesser problem would not justify troubling the king, though some understand it in other ways.

Esther speaks before King Ahasuerus at the second banquet. Until now she had kept secret that she was Jewish. Haman, a high official, had obtained a decree to exterminate the Jews. Esther risks her life by revealing her identity and asking the king for help.

For today: when you see an injustice and have a voice or influence, do not hide. Ask God for wisdom and courage to speak with respect, at the right moment, and on behalf of those who cannot defend themselves.
exp.7:10:
This verse says that the king allowed the Jews in every city to gather together and defend their lives. They could destroy and kill any armed force of a people or province that attacked them, including little ones and women, and take their goods as plunder.

Here the text describes the decree of King Ahasuerus, written at the command of Mordecai. Earlier, Haman had obtained a law to wipe out the Jews, and that law could not be revoked. So another decree was issued that allowed them to defend themselves. Some understand the phrase about little ones and women to describe those who would attack them, while others see an expression that reflects the wording of the first decree. Scholars interpret it in several ways.

For today: when you face injustice, look for paths of protection and justice without hatred, trusting that God cares for his people.
exp.1:5:
The verse says that Mordecai, the Jew who lived in Susa, had been carried away from Jerusalem along with the captives whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon deported together with Jeconiah, king of Judah. Being carried away by force to another place is what the verse describes, and the captives are the prisoners taken in war.

The one who speaks is the narrator of the book, who introduces Mordecai by explaining where his family comes from. There is a detail that can be understood in two ways: some think the exile was Mordecai himself, and others think it was his great-grandfather Kish, because the years do not fit well. The text does not fully settle the matter.

For today: God can use people who live far from their land and their comfort. If you feel out of place, your situation is not an obstacle to God working through you.
exp.6:6:
This verse says that the king got up from the banquet full of anger and went out into the palace garden. Haman stayed behind to beg Queen Esther to spare his life, because he understood that the king had already decided to punish him. The "garden" mentioned here is the palace grounds, and the king's "anger" was a strong rage. In this verse, "make request" means to plead earnestly.

Esther had just accused Haman before King Ahasuerus of being the enemy who wanted to destroy her people. The king went out to calm down and think. Haman, with no way out, tried to plead with the one person who could intercede for him, the very woman he had threatened.

For today: sooner or later, what we sow catches up with us. Haman lived with pride and wickedness, and in the end he had no one to turn to. It is worth living with humility and justice, and asking for forgiveness in time, before the crisis arrives.
exp.8:3:
This verse says that Mordecai held a position of great importance in the king's palace. His fame spread throughout the whole kingdom, and his power kept growing. The phrase "waxed greater and greater" means that he became more and more influential.

Here the narrator of the book of Esther speaks. He explains why no one dared to oppose the Jews on the day they could defend themselves: the officials of the kingdom knew that Mordecai was a respected authority, and for that reason they supported them. The text shows a complete change, since Mordecai had been threatened with death and now he was honored.

For today: God can change very difficult situations and use faithful people in places of influence. If you are in a position of responsibility, use it with integrity and to protect others, not only for your own benefit.
exp.2:11:
Esther 3:12 tells us that the king's scribes were called together on the thirteenth day of the first month. There they wrote down everything Haman commanded. The letters were addressed to the king's lieutenants, to the governors over every province, and to the rulers of every people in every province, each according to its writing and each people in its own language. They were written in the name of King Ahasuerus and sealed with the king's ring.

Haman, a high official, hated the Jews. The king had given him his ring, which served as the official seal, and with it he gave him enormous authority. In this way, the order to destroy the Jews became law of the kingdom, and it could not easily be changed.

For today: words and decisions carry great power, especially when authority is used. If we have influence, let us use it to protect and not to harm. And when we see injustice, let us remember that God is not indifferent, even though his work is not yet visible here.
exp.3:2:
This verse says that in every province where the king's command and decree arrived, the Jews went into very deep grief. They fasted, they wept, and they lamented. Sackcloth was a rough cloth worn in times of mourning, and ashes were also a sign of sorrow. Many lay in sackcloth and ashes.

This is part of the story of the book of Esther, not a speech. Haman had obtained a decree to destroy the Jews throughout the Persian empire. Mordecai, Esther's cousin and guardian, learned of it and showed his anguish openly. The people did the same in every place. These acts expressed grief and also a plea before God, although the text here does not mention his name.

When news comes that crushes us, we do not have to pretend to be strong. We can weep and pray honestly, and seek out other believers so that we do not carry the pain alone. Often God uses those moments to move us to act, as happened with Esther.
exp.1:19:
Esther had still not told anyone what people she came from or who her relatives were, because Mordecai had ordered her to keep it secret. She kept obeying him just as she had when he raised her as a child. The phrase "she was being raised" means she was brought up under his care.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Esther was already queen of Persia, but Mordecai, her cousin and guardian, was still guiding her. The text does not explain why he asked for that silence. Some think he wanted to protect her, and others think he wanted to wait for the right moment. What we do see is that, shortly afterward, Mordecai uncovers a plot against the king.

For today: even when we reach places of success or responsibility, it is wise to stay humble and willing to listen to the advice of wise people. That attitude protects us and can prepare us for whatever God does next.
exp.8:4:
This verse says that the Jews defeated all their enemies with violence: sword, death, and destruction. A "stroke of the sword" means a hard blow from a weapon, and "destruction" means total ruin. "Did what they would unto those that hated them" means they acted freely against those who had attacked them.

It is part of the story of Esther. The narrator tells of the day on which, according to Haman's decree, the enemies were going to destroy the Jews. The king allowed the Jews to defend themselves. The officials supported them out of fear of Mordecai. The text describes what happened; it does not say that God approved of every act. Interpreters discuss how to understand the harshness of this passage.

For today: let us learn to trust that God cares for his people, but let us seek to defend ourselves and to defend others with justice, without revenge or cruelty.
exp.1:10:
This verse says that Mordecai walked back and forth every day in front of the courtyard where the king's women's house was. He wanted to know how Esther was doing and what was happening to her. The word "walked back and forth" means he kept pacing up and down, and the phrase "what was happening to her" means what was going on with her.

The narrator is the one telling us this. Esther, a young Jewish woman, had been taken into the Persian palace, and Mordecai, her relative who had raised her, had asked her not to reveal her people. He could not go inside, but he stayed close by to watch over her well-being. Many interpret this as a father's care, though the text does not say more.

Today we can learn to steadily stand by those we love, even when we cannot control their situation. A phone call, a visit, or a daily prayer can be a real way of caring.
exp.5:5:
This verse tells how Haman comes in before the king, and the king asks him what should be done for the man whom the king wants to honor. Haman thinks to himself: "To whom would the king delight to do honor more than to myself?" The word "honor" here means public recognition and respect.

The narrator speaks, and then King Ahasuerus and Haman. That night the king could not sleep, he read the records and discovered that Mordecai had saved his life without receiving any reward. Haman had come to ask for Mordecai's death, but without knowing it, the king wants to honor exactly that man.

For today: pride makes us believe that all praise is for us, and it blinds us to what God is doing. We can ask him for a humble heart, one that rejoices when others are recognized and does not always seek to be the center.
exp.2:4:
What it says: Haman noticed that Mordecai did not bow down or pay him homage, and he was filled with fury. The phrases "bowed down" and "paid homage" describe making a deep bow, as a sign of respect and submission. The word "saw" is spelled differently in the older text but means the same thing.

Context: The narrator tells us that the king had ordered that Haman, his high official, be honored. Mordecai, who was a Jew, refused, and the king's servants reported him. The text does not explain the exact reason for his refusal. Some think it was out of loyalty to God, others because of the history of enmity between his people and the Amalekites, since Haman is called an Agagite. This is an interpretation, not something stated clearly here.

For today: Wounded pride can grow until it becomes destructive. Before reacting with anger, let us ask God to help us calm our hearts and not let our ego guide us.
exp.0:17:
This verse says that the noblewomen of Persia and Media, upon learning what Queen Vashti did, would talk about it before the king's princes. The result would be "contempt and wrath": the wives would look down on their husbands, and the husbands would become angry. "Ladies" are the women of the nobility; "heard" means "listen to"; "contempt" is a lack of respect.

The speaker is Memucan, a counselor of King Ahasuerus. Vashti refused to appear before the king during a banquet. Memucan exaggerates the case, fearing that the event will harm the authority of men, and proposes stripping her of the title of queen. It is the advice of a man concerned about his own position, not a teaching from God.

For today: be careful not to let the fear of losing prestige or control lead us into exaggerated reactions. Respect in the home is not achieved through laws or impositions, but through love, dialogue, and dignified treatment.
exp.0:18:
Memucan proposes to the king an official decree: that it be written among the laws of Persia and Media, so that it cannot be changed. The decree would be that Vashti must never again come before King Ahasuerus, and that the king give her royal position to another woman who is better than she is.

The speaker is Memucan, one of the king's advisers. Vashti refused to appear at the banquet, and he fears that other wives will do the same and that there will be disrespect in households. This is his own opinion, and the text does not present it as wise counsel from God. It is a political reaction, shaped by wounded pride and fear.

For today: when someone offends us or challenges us, let us not make decisions driven by pride or fear. Before acting, let us pray and ask for wisdom. God invites us to seek respect through love and good example, not through control.
exp.3:14:
This verse says that Esther sent an answer back to Mordecai. The wording the verse refers to is not in the verse your reader sees, so I have left it out. The verse only announces that she is going to respond, and her actual reply appears in the next verse.

Esther is the queen of Persia, and she is Jewish. Mordecai, her relative who raised her, asked her to speak to the king to save their people from death. Entering the king's presence without being called could cost her her life. She does not answer with an excuse but with a decision, and before she acts she asks that everyone pray and fast.

For today: before making a difficult decision, do not act in a hurry or rely only on your own strength. Seek out other believers who will pray with you, and ask God for courage and wisdom.
exp.0:11:
This verse tells that Queen Vashti refused to come when the king sent for her through his eunuchs (court officials). "To come" here means to present herself before someone. The king became very angry, and his anger burned within him, meaning he was filled with fury.

The narrator relates what happened on the seventh day of a great banquet, when King Ahasuerus was merry with wine. He wanted Vashti to come wearing her crown to show her beauty to everyone. The text does not explain why she refused, and for that reason various interpretations have been given. What we do see is the king's reaction, which sets up what follows in the story.

For today: when something upsets or hurts us, it is wise to pause before acting. Anger that runs unchecked, especially in the midst of excess, often leads to decisions we later regret. Let us ask God for calm and wisdom.
exp.1:9:
The verse says Esther had not revealed her people or her family. She did this because her cousin Mordecai, who had raised her, had told her to keep silent about it. The word "shewed" in the King James Version means to make known or to tell openly.

The book presents this as a fact. Esther, a young Jewish woman, now lives in the palace of the Persian king, in Susa, among many young women gathered for the king. Mordecai gives her this instruction, but the text does not explain his reasons. Some think he wanted to protect her from prejudice against the Jews; others think he was preparing for what would come later. We cannot know this for certain.

There are times when God calls us to wisdom and not to speak about everything right away. Listening to the advice of wise and trustworthy people helps us decide when to keep quiet and when to speak, trusting that God is at work even in what we do not understand.
exp.2:3:
This verse says that the king's servants kept urging Mordecai every day to obey the order to bow before Haman, but he would not listen to them. So they reported to Haman, to see whether Mordecai would stand firm in his decision, since he had already told them he was a Jew. The word used for "told" in the verse means that they informed on him, which is to say they reported him.

This is the narrator of the book speaking. Haman was the highest-ranking man in the kingdom, and the king had commanded that everyone kneel before him. Mordecai refused. The text does not explain his reason in detail; it only says that he is a Jew. Some think it was a matter of his faith, but the text does not make this clear.

Today it teaches us that holding to our convictions can bring constant pressure. Let us ask God for wisdom and steadfastness to act with integrity, without seeking conflict, trusting that he cares for his own.
exp.2:12:
This verse tells that letters were sent by messengers to all the provinces of the kingdom. They ordered that all Jews be destroyed, killed, and wiped out, from the children to the elderly, including the women, in a single day: the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, called Adar. They also allowed the attackers to take their possessions.

The narrator describes what Haman, a high official of King Ahasuerus, did. He was offended because Mordecai, a Jew, would not bow down before him. Haman convinced the king to approve the plan, and the decree was sealed with the royal signet ring, which gave it authority. The book shows the danger that the Jewish people faced in Persia.

Today it reminds us that hatred can hide behind authority and unjust laws. We can reject all prejudice and courageously defend those who are mistreated. We can also trust that God continues to care for his people, even when we cannot see it clearly.
exp.0:14:
Here the king asks his advisers what the law requires be done with Queen Vashti. She did not carry out the king's command, which had been sent to her through the chamberlains, who were trusted officials at the court. Asuerus is Ahasuerus, and Vasti is Vashti.

The king speaks with seven princes of Persia and Media, wise in the law and the times, who were close to him. Vashti had refused to appear before the king during a banquet. The text does not explain why she refused, so we should not invent a reason. The king, angry, seeks legal counsel.

For today: before reacting in anger, it is wise to seek wise counsel and think about the consequences. Here the question sounds calm, but the decision that follows is harsh. Let us ask God for humility and self-control.
exp.7:0:
That same day King Ahasuerus gave to Queen Esther everything that had belonged to Haman, the enemy of the Jews. It also says that Mordecai came before the king, because Esther had told him who Mordecai was to her. The words "gave" and "unto" are old forms of the modern words that appear in the verse above, "gave" and "to." The word "told" means that she explained to the king the relationship they had.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Haman had been put to death after planning the destruction of the Jewish people. According to the text, Mordecai was Esther's cousin and had raised her. Now the king acknowledges Mordecai and begins to restore what had been turned upside down. The account does not say how much the king knew before this.

For today: God can change unjust situations, and sometimes He does so through brave and sincere people. If He has placed you in a place of influence, use your voice honestly to help others.
exp.9:0:
This verse says that King Ahasuerus (also known as Xerxes, according to many scholars) placed a tax on his whole kingdom, including the lands along the coast and the islands of the sea. "Laid a tribute" means he required the payment of a levy to the government. The phrase "the isles of the sea" refers to distant regions, near the sea.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, not a character. After telling how the Jewish people were saved, the book briefly shows the king's power. It then highlights Mordecai, who became second only to the king and used his position to seek the good of his people. Why the tax is mentioned is not clear; some believe it shows the stability of the kingdom.

For today: power and money pass away, but what remains is using our influence, great or small, to serve others and to pursue peace.
exp.8:22:
This verse says that the Jews agreed to keep celebrating what they had already begun to do, just as Mordecai had asked them in writing. "Accepted" means they received it gladly and committed themselves to doing it every year.

The one speaking here is the narrator of the book. Mordecai had sent letters so that the people would remember each year their deliverance from Haman's plans. The festival, called Purim, was born so that they would not forget how their sorrow turned into joy. The verses that follow explain the reason for the festival.

For today: let us not allow the memory of what God has done for us to be lost. We can set aside regular moments, such as a family meal or a prayer of thanksgiving, to remember his blessings and share joy with others, especially those in need.
exp.0:15:
Memucan speaks before the king and the princes. He says that Queen Vashti has wronged not only the king, but also all the princes and all the peoples in the provinces of the kingdom. The word "wrong" here is used in the sense of having done an injury or a serious offense against the authority.

Memucan was one of the seven counselor princes. The king asked for their opinion about what to do with Vashti, who refused to come before him. Memucan exaggerates the matter, turning a conflict within the royal household into a threat to the whole empire. The text does not say whether his motive was sincere or whether he was trying to protect his own position, so it is best not to claim either.

For today: let us be careful not to enlarge problems with exaggerated words. Advice given out of fear or pride can lead to hasty decisions. Before we speak, let us ask God for wisdom, and speak with truth and calm.
exp.7:16:
Wherever the king's new order arrived, the Jews celebrated with joy, feasting, and festivity. The word "joy" here refers to celebration, as the verse itself says "joy and gladness." Also, many people from other peoples became identified with the Jews, because they feared them.

The narrator of the book of Esther tells what happened after the king allowed the Jews to defend themselves against Haman's plan to destroy them. Their lives had been in danger, and now they were delivered. Scholars are not sure whether those people truly converted or only sought to protect themselves.

Today we can remember that God cares for his people even when he is not obviously seen. When he delivers us from something difficult, it is worth pausing, giving thanks, and celebrating with others.
exp.3:3:
She says that Esther's maids and her chamberlains came and told her what was happening with Mordecai. Esther was deeply distressed, and she sent clothing so that he would take off the sackcloth, which was a rough cloth worn as a sign of mourning. But Mordecai did not accept it.

It is part of Esther's story, written in the third person. Mordecai was in public mourning because the king's decree threatened all the Jews. Esther, who lived inside the palace, did not yet know the reason. She wanted to ease his grief with clothing, but he was not looking for a quick comfort: his sorrow had a serious cause.

For today: when someone suffers, we sometimes want to fix the appearance of the problem with something quick. It is wise to listen first, as Esther will do later, and to understand what lies behind the pain before offering solutions.
exp.8:11:
Here King Ahasuerus tells Queen Esther what he has been informed: in Shushan, the capital, the Jews killed five hundred men and the ten sons of Haman. Then he wonders what has happened in the rest of the provinces, and he offers Esther whatever she asks for.

The king speaks after Haman, an enemy of the Jews, had planned to destroy them. Since the first decree could not be reversed, the king allowed the Jews to defend themselves. Esther receives once again an open offer, and in the next verse she asks for one more day in Shushan. Some readers are troubled by this request, and the text does not fully explain it.

For today: when God places us in a position of influence, it is good to use it with courage and wisdom, asking clearly and keeping in mind the protection of the vulnerable.
exp.1:4:
Mordecai is introduced, a Jew who lived in Shushan, one of the cities where the king of Persia stayed. His ancestors are named as Jair, Shimei, and Kish, of the tribe of Benjamin. "Man" means a male person, and "palace" refers to the place where the king lives.

The narrator of the book introduces a key character. Jews were living far from their land after the exile. The following verse says that someone from his family was taken captive from Jerusalem. It is not entirely clear whether it refers to Mordecai or to Kish, and scholars explain it in different ways.

God can use ordinary people who live far from home or in difficult circumstances. Wherever you find yourself today, be faithful and honor your origin and your faith, because God can work through you.
exp.0:12:
This verse says that King Ahasuerus, angry because Queen Vashti had refused to come, consulted the wise men. These were men who "knew the times," that is, they understood the periods of history and matters of the law. The text makes clear that the king had the custom of consulting experts in law and judgment before deciding.

The narrator of the book explains this custom in the middle of the story. The king is furious and wants an official answer. The seven princes of Persia and Media, who are close to him, will give him counsel. Some scholars think that "knew the times" refers to knowing precedents, or even to astrologers, but the text does not specify this.

For today: asking for counsel is wise, but it is good to do so calmly. Ahasuerus asked for advice while angry, and that may have influenced what was decided. Before deciding something important, slow down, pray, and seek out wise and just voices.
exp.6:4:
King Ahasuerus asks Esther: "Who is he, and where is he, that would dare do such a thing?" The phrase "durst presume in his heart" is an old one and means that someone had filled himself with boldness or courage to act. The king did not know who had planned the ruin of Esther's people, and he wants to know who he is.

King Ahasuerus speaks, surprised and indignant. Esther has just revealed to him, with great care and respect, that she and her people have been sold to be destroyed. Up to that moment Ahasuerus did not know that his decree affected the queen. His question opens the way for Esther to point to Haman.

For today: Esther spoke at the right moment, with respect and without fear of the truth, even at the risk of her life. When we must defend others or say something difficult, we can pray, wait for the right moment, and speak with clarity and humility.
exp.8:29:
This verse says that Mordecai sent letters to all the Jews who lived in the one hundred twenty-seven provinces of King Ahasuerus. The word "letters" means written messages or documents. And "words of peace and truth" means messages of calm and sincerity, not of threat or deception.

The narrator of the book tells how Mordecai and Queen Esther wanted the people to remember their deliverance every year. After having been in danger of being destroyed, they were now asked to celebrate Purim. Mordecai did not impose the feast harshly, but with a peaceful and truthful message. Some scholars see here a tone of reconciliation and unity.

For today: when you have to correct, invite, or remind others of something, do it with words of peace and truth. Being sincere does not have to be harsh, and being kind does not mean keeping silent about the truth.
exp.4:7:
Esther tells the king that if he is pleased with her and wants to grant what she asks, he should come with Haman to a second banquet that she will prepare. There she will give her answer. "Having found favor in the eyes" means having made a good impression on him, having his good will. "Petition" is what she is requesting. "I will prepare" means "I will get ready."

She is Queen Esther, a young Jewish woman. King Ahasuerus offered her up to half the kingdom, but she does not yet reveal her request. Her people are in danger because of Haman's plan. Many think she is waiting for the right moment; the text does not fully explain her reasons.

For today: one does not always have to say everything at once. Before taking an important step, pray, think calmly, and look for the right moment and the right way, trusting that God guides the process.
exp.4:2:
Here the king Ahasuerus asks Esther what is troubling her and what she wishes to request of him. He promises to give her up to half of the kingdom. The king speaks after Esther came into his presence without being called, which could have cost her her life. He extended the golden scepter and so showed her his favor. The phrase "up to half of the kingdom" seems to be an expression of generosity rather than a literal offer. Esther does not yet ask for what she truly needs, but instead invites the king and Haman to a banquet. Many understand that she acts with caution and wisdom, although the text does not explain all her motives.

When you face something difficult, pray and ask God for direction before acting. Sometimes wisdom consists in waiting for the right moment and speaking with prudence, trusting that God works in every step.
exp.9:1:
It says that all the powerful and courageous deeds of Mordecai, together with the account of his great rise by the king's will, are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia. "Chronicles" refers to records kept year by year. The question "are they not written?" invites the reader to check it, as if to say: "This is on record in the archives."

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Esther, closing the story. After mentioning the taxes imposed by King Ahasuerus, he notes that Mordecai was second in authority to him. We do not know for certain whether that Persian chronicle book survives today; the text mentions it only as a reference.

For today: a person's true worth lies not only in power but in using it for the good of others, as Mordecai did, seeking the welfare of his people. Strive to serve with what God has given you.
exp.4:12:
Haman says that although he has riches, children, honor, and a special place with the king and queen, none of it gives him any satisfaction as long as he sees Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king's gate. "All this availeth me nothing" means that it does him no good and brings him no joy. The king's gate was the place where Mordecai carried on his business, and he would not bow down to Haman.

Haman speaks to his friends and to his wife Zeresh, after leaving Esther's banquet. He is proud, but his pride is also wounded. One man who does not give him honor poisons everything for him. This leads him to accept the plan to hang Mordecai.

For today: when pride and envy rule us, no blessing is enough. It is wise to be thankful for what God has given us and to hand over our resentments before they grow and destroy us.
exp.1:21:
Mordecai learned of the plot of the two officers to kill the king. Then he told Queen Esther, and she warned the king, saying that the news came from Mordecai.

The words "knowing this" mean "when he realized this." "Reported" means that he informed the king, and "in the name of" indicates that Esther gave the credit to him.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, without quoting anyone. Mordecai was sitting at the palace gate, a place where official matters were handled. Esther still kept silent about her Jewish origin, as he had asked her to. This event was recorded in the chronicles of the kingdom, and later it will become very important in the story.

For today: when someone helps you or contributes something valuable, acknowledge it honestly and give credit to the one who deserves it. Doing what is right, even when no one notices, is never lost.
exp.4:8:
This verse says that Haman left the palace happy and in good spirits, because the queen had invited him to a banquet with the king. But when he saw Mordecai at the king's gate, not standing up or showing him respect, he was filled with anger.

The narrator tells what happened after Esther asked that the king and Haman come to a banquet. Haman was a high official of the kingdom. Mordecai, a Jew, did not bow before him. The Bible does not explain the reason in detail here, so we should not claim more than the text says.

For today: good news can make us glad, but a single resentment can take away our peace. It is worth examining what we allow to grow in our hearts. Let us ask God for humility so that we do not live dependent on the recognition of others.
exp.3:5:
He says that Hatach, a eunuch in the king's service, went out to meet Mordecai. He found him in the street of the city, in front of the king's gate. The phrase "So Hatach went forth" means "then Hatach went out," and "street" refers to an open, public space within the city.

Esther had just learned that Mordecai was dressed in sackcloth as a sign of mourning. Since he refused the clothing she had sent him, she sent Hatach, a man she trusted, to find out what was happening and why. The verse tells how that order was carried out. Mordecai was still near the king's gate, though in mourning clothes he could not enter it.

When someone is suffering, quick solutions, like the clothing Esther sent, are sometimes not enough. We need to draw near, listen, and understand the problem at its root. Ask with interest and listen with patience.
exp.1:7:
This verse tells us that when King Ahasuerus gave the command to gather many young women in Shushan, the capital city, Esther was also taken into the palace. She was placed under the care of Hegai, the official in charge of the king's women.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, and he does not mention God, but he shows how Esther, a young orphaned Jewish woman raised by her cousin Mordecai, arrives at a place of power. The text does not say whether she went of her own will or by compulsion; interpreters understand it in different ways. What is clear is that the story is preparing her later role.

For today: sometimes we find ourselves in places we did not choose. Even there, God can work quietly, and we can live with wisdom, trusting that our lives have a purpose.
exp.8:24:
This verse sums up how the situation changed. When Esther came before the king, he ordered in writing that Haman's wicked plan against the Jews should fall back on Haman's own head. He also commanded that he and his sons be hanged on the gallows. "Commanded" means ordered or instructed. "Plan" means scheme or device.

The one speaking here is the narrator of the book, who tells how King Ahasuerus responded to Esther's request. Haman had planned to destroy the Jews and had cast lots (Pur) to choose the date. The passage explains why the Jews celebrate Purim: they remember that God, through Esther and Mordecai, delivered them. Some scholars note that the text speaks of Haman's hanging, but also of his sons, and not all agree on the details.

For today: trust that God can change unjust situations. Ask for courage to act with wisdom when someone needs your voice, as Esther did.
exp.4:0:
On the third day, it says, Esther put on her royal clothing and stood in the inner court of the palace, facing the king's house. The king was sitting on his royal throne in the royal house, facing the entrance. The throne is named in the verse as the royal throne, and "the royal house" refers to the king's hall or chamber in the palace.

The narrator of the book tells us this. Esther had asked the Jews to fast for three days on her behalf (Esther 4:16), because entering the king's presence without being called could cost her her life. Now, after those days have passed, she takes the step. The text does not say what she felt, but it is clear that she acts with courage.

For today: when you have to face something difficult, prepare yourself with prayer and the support of others, and then take the step. Courage is not the absence of fear, but moving forward after you have prepared.
exp.3:9:
This verse says that Esther spoke to Hathach, the king's attendant who carried messages, and gave him instructions to bring back an answer to Mordecai. Esther does not speak directly with her cousin but through this messenger.

Mordecai had asked Esther to go before the king to plead for her people, the Jews, who were threatened with death by a decree. Esther now begins her reply, and in the verses that follow she explains the danger: entering the king's presence without being called could cost her life.

For today: when God asks us for something difficult, it is natural to feel afraid and to express that fear honestly. Esther did not keep silent or pretend to be brave; she spoke plainly. We can do the same in prayer and with trusted people, and seek counsel before taking the next step.
exp.5:8:
Here Haman tells King Ahasuerus how to honor someone. He asks that a royal robe and one of the king's horses be given to one of the most noble princes, so that he may dress that man and lead him on horseback through the city square. In front of him, a herald will announce that this is how the one whom the king wishes to honor is to be treated.

Haman is speaking, the most powerful man after the king. He believes the king wants to honor him, so he describes the greatest honor he can imagine. But the king was referring to Mordecai, the Jew whom Haman hated. So Haman himself has to do what he proposed.

For today: pride deceives us and makes us seek applause. Better that we serve with humility, trusting that God knows when and how to honor each person.
exp.2:7:
Haman speaks to King Ahasuerus and describes the Jews as a people scattered and divided among all the provinces. He says their laws are different, that they do not keep the king's laws, and that for this reason it is not good for the king to let them live.

Haman speaks out of hatred toward Mordecai and his people. He does not name them: he says "a certain people" without saying which one. He mixes a half-truth (the Jews had customs of their own) with an exaggerated accusation (that they did not obey the king). In this way he seeks to have the king sign a decree without investigating.

For today: let us be wary of those who describe an entire group with generalizations and suspicions. Before repeating or believing an accusation, let us ask for the facts and treat each person with justice, remembering that God sees and cares for his people even when they seem threatened.
exp.4:5:
The verse tells how King Ahasuerus, while they were at the banquet of wine, asks Esther what she wants. He assures her that he will grant it, and even uses a phrase of generosity: "even to the half of the kingdom." What she wants to ask for and what she wants are almost the same idea: what she desires to request.

The king speaks, and he does so for the second time, since he had already made a similar offer before. Esther had come before him without being summoned, which was risky, and he received her with favor. She prepared a banquet and also invited Haman, the enemy of her people. Many understand this waiting of Esther as prudence: she is looking for the right moment. The Bible does not explain all of her reasons.

For today: before acting in a difficult situation, pray, think, and wait with wisdom. God can guide you to choose the right moment, without rushing or being paralyzed by fear.
exp.6:2:
Esther speaks to the king with respect. She says, "If I have found favour in thy sight," that is, if she has his favor, and "if it please the king," meaning if it seems good to him. Then she asks for two things: that her life be granted to her, and the life of her people. "Petition" and "request" are two ways of saying what she asks for.

Esther is the Jewish queen in Persia. She is at the second banquet with King Ahasuerus and Haman. Until now she had kept her origin a secret, but now, risking her life, she reveals that her people are condemned to die by a decree that Haman promoted.

Esther does not accuse in anger, but speaks with humility, clarity and courage. When we must defend others or speak about something unjust, we can do it with respect, with truth, and trusting in God, even if it is frightening.
exp.2:9:
The verse says that King Ahasuerus took his ring from his hand and gave it to Haman, who is described as "the son of Hammedatha the Agagite" and "the Jews' enemy." The ring served as a seal: with it the king's orders were signed, and no one could change them. The word for "gave it" in the verse is simply "gave it."

Haman had just accused the Jews before the king. He presented them as a separate people who did not obey the laws, and he offered money to destroy them. The king investigated nothing and gave Haman his authority. Some believe that "Agagite" connects him with Agag, king of the Amalekites, though this is not known with certainty.

For today: before believing an accusation against someone, let us listen calmly and seek the truth. Well-chosen words can hide hatred, and injustice grows when no one asks questions.
exp.1:6:
This verse tells how Mordecai raised his cousin Hadassah, also called Esther, because she had been left an orphan. It says she was a young woman of fair form and good appearance, that is, pleasing in figure and face. When her parents died, Mordecai took her as his own daughter. Hadassah is her Hebrew name; Esther is the name by which she became known afterward.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, and his name is not given. He introduces Esther before she is taken to the palace. Both are Jews living in Susa, far from their homeland, descendants of those carried into exile in Babylon. The text does not explain every detail, but it shows that Esther did not come to that situation alone.

For today: God can use those who lovingly care for others without being their parents. Think of someone who needs your support, and help them with steadiness and tenderness.
exp.0:8:
This verse tells us that Queen Vashti also made a feast of her own, only for the women, in the royal house of King Ahasuerus. While the king was giving a great feast for the men, she was hosting the guests among the women. The word "also" here means "too" or "in the same way."

The Book of Esther narrates what happened in the Persian empire. Here the narrator describes the king's feast, which lasted many days and had plenty of wine and luxury. This detail sets up what follows: when the king is cheerful from the wine, he sends for Vashti, and from there the story takes a very important turn.

For today: decisions made in the middle of a feast or of excess can have serious consequences. This invites us to act with calm and wisdom, and to remember that God works even in disordered situations.
exp.0:9:
On the seventh day of the banquet, when King Ahasuerus was already cheerful and merry from wine, he gave an order to seven officials who attended him closely. These officials were members of the royal court, men who served the king directly. Here "commanded" means that he gave an order. The seven are named one by one.

It is the narrator of the book who tells this. The banquet had lasted a full week, and the king had allowed each person to drink as they pleased. What follows shows that he gave the order with his judgment clouded by wine: he wanted to display the beauty of Queen Vashti. The text does not say whether wine was the only cause, but it does mark the moment.

For today: decisions made in a moment of excitement, or under the influence of something that clouds judgment, can bring painful consequences. Before giving an order or speaking with authority, it is wise to pause and think calmly.
exp.3:0:
Mordecai learns of everything that had happened: the king had signed a decree to destroy the Jews. Then he tears his clothes, puts on rough clothing as a sign of mourning, and covers himself with ashes, signs of deep grief in that time. He goes out through the city crying out loudly, with a strong cry full of bitterness.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Esther. Mordecai was a Jew and the cousin and guardian of Esther, the queen. The decree, promoted by Haman, put all his people in danger throughout the Persian empire. His public reaction shows anguish, and the verses that follow say that many Jews did the same.

For today: when pain or injustice strikes you, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can express your sadness honestly, and then seek God and act with courage, as Mordecai will do later.
exp.5:4:
The servants tell the king that Haman is standing in the court. King Ahasuerus, not knowing why Haman has come, gives a single command: "Let him come in." The "court" was the outer courtyard of the palace, and the "servants" were the officials who attended the king.

The king could not sleep, and he had asked for the records of the kingdom to be read to him. There he learned that Mordecai had uncovered a plot against his life and had never been rewarded. Just then Haman arrived, very early in the morning, to ask that Mordecai be hanged on the gallows he had prepared. The servants only report who is outside; they do not know what is about to happen.

God is not named in the book of Esther, but many see his care in these well-timed events. Today we can remember that God keeps working even when we cannot see it. If you are going through an unjust or confusing situation, trust that he can change things at the right moment, and in the meantime keep doing what is right with patience.
exp.9:2:
This verse says that Mordecai the Jew was second in importance after King Ahasuerus. He was great among the Jews and loved by most of his fellow countrymen. He sought the good of his people and spoke peace to all his descendants. The words "accepted" and "seed" are rewritten here: "accepted" means well received or held dear, and "seed" means descendants.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Esther, who closes the story. Mordecai had helped save the Jews from Haman's decree of destruction. Now the account shows that his power did not end in personal pride, but was used to protect and encourage his people. The author is not named with certainty.

For today: if God gives us influence, at work, in the family, or in the church, let us use it to serve and to promote peace, not to show off. Let us seek the good of others with words that build up.
exp.3:11:
This verse is very brief: it tells that the messengers brought Mordecai Esther's answer. "They told" here means they reported or passed on her words.

Mordecai had asked Esther to speak with the king to save the Jews from the sentence of death. Esther, through Hatach, explained that entering before the king without being called could cost her life, and that she had not been called to the king for thirty days. She was not refusing out of coldness, but was honestly describing the real danger.

For today: when God places us before a difficult decision, there is nothing wrong with honestly expressing our fears. What matters is not to remain there, but to keep listening, to seek wise counsel, and to ask for the courage to obey.
exp.8:26:
This verse says that the Jews firmly resolved that they, their descendants, and all who joined themselves to their people would keep these two days every year, as it was written and at its appointed time. "Descendants" is what the word "seed" means here. "Those who join themselves to them" refers to those who become part of their community. The phrase "shall not fail" means the custom would never be allowed to lapse.

The one who speaks is the narrator of the book. He tells how, after God delivered them from Haman's plan, the Jews agreed to keep the feast of Purim. They wanted their children and future generations to remember that deliverance and not forget it.

For today: remember with gratitude what God has done for us. We can build simple habits, such as giving thanks together as a family or telling our children how God helped us, so that faith and memory are passed on to the next generation.
exp.1:22:
This verse tells us that the plot against King Ahasuerus was investigated and found to be true. The two guilty officers were hanged on a tree, that is, they were publicly executed. Furthermore, the matter was written down in the book of the chronicles, which were the official records of the kingdom. The phrase "when inquisition was made" means that an inquiry was carried out, and "it was found out" means that the charge was confirmed.

Here the narrator of the book of Esther is speaking. Mordecai had discovered the plan and alerted Esther, and she told the king. This record may seem like a minor detail, but later, in Esther 6, that same book will be read to the king and will bring about an important turn in the story. In this way, without mentioning God, we see how things are gradually falling into place.

For today: do what is right even when no one acknowledges it. God sees what we do in silence, and he can use in his own time what seemed forgotten.
exp.5:2:
Here King Ahasuerus asks what reward Mordecai received for having uncovered a plot against the king's life. "Honour" and "dignity" refer to recognition and reward. The servants answer that nothing was done for him, that is, no one rewarded him.

The king could not sleep, and he ordered that the book of the chronicles be read to him. There he found that Mordecai had reported two eunuchs who had wanted to kill him. The king realizes that this debt was left unpaid. Shortly afterward Haman arrives to ask for Mordecai's death. The text does not mention God, but many readers see here his quiet care in a sleepless night.

For today: God can watch over the details of our lives without our noticing. Do good faithfully, even when no one acknowledges it, and trust that God sees and knows how to act in his time.
exp.0:3:
This verse says that King Ahasuerus wanted to show the riches of the glory of his kingdom and the splendor of his great power. He did so over many days: one hundred and eighty, that is, about six months.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, telling what King Ahasuerus did (many identify him with Xerxes I of Persia, although the text does not say so). He was in Susa, the capital, and he gathered his princes, servants, and governors. The account presents human power in all its brilliance, and so it sets the stage for what will happen next with Esther.

For today: it is easy to impress others with what we have or achieve. This passage invites us to ask what we boast in and what we trust. Human kingdoms, however great they seem, pass away. Let us instead seek the glory that comes from God and live with humility.
exp.7:3:
Here the king Ahasuerus holds out his golden scepter toward Esther, which was the sign that she could come near and speak without danger. She gets up and stands before him.

The passage describes what happens. Esther had already been weeping at the king's feet, pleading with him to cancel Haman's plan against the Jews. Although Haman had already fallen, his decree was still in force. With the scepter, the king gives her permission to keep speaking, and she will now present her formal request.

For today: when someone with more power opens the door for us, it is wise to speak with respect, courage, and clarity. Esther did not stay silent in the face of her people's suffering. We too can intercede for others with humility and firmness, and pray trusting that God hears us.
exp.8:1:
It says that on the thirteenth day of Adar, the Jews gathered together in their cities, throughout all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, to defend themselves against those who sought to harm them. To lay hand on such as sought their hurt means to attack or act forcefully against someone. No one could stand against them, because a great fear of them had fallen upon all the peoples.

Here the narrator of the book of Esther speaks. Earlier, Haman had obtained a decree to destroy the Jews on that very day. Since Persian laws could not be revoked, the king allowed the Jews to defend themselves. The account shows how the situation turned completely around.

For today: God can change situations that seem lost. When we face injustice or threats, we can act with courage and wisdom, and trust that God works even when we do not see it directly.
exp.7:1:
This verse says that the king took off the ring, the same one he had recovered from Haman, and gave it to Mordecai. Also, Esther put him in charge of the property of Haman's house. The word "took off" is the verb in the verse, and the phrase "gave it" is the verb in the verse as well, while the phrase "over the house" means that he was made the manager of everything that had belonged to Haman.

This is part of the story of Esther. Haman had planned to destroy the Jews and had already been executed. King Ahasuerus handed Esther the house of Haman, and Esther revealed her kinship with Mordecai. The ring was used to seal decrees with royal authority, so Mordecai received a position of trust. Even so, the danger to the Jews had not yet passed.

For today: God can change unjust situations, but he often expects us to act with courage and wisdom. Let us humbly use any influence we receive to serve and protect others.
exp.3:13:
Mordecai tells Esther that if she stays silent at this time, relief and deliverance for the Jews will come from another place, but she and her father's house will be destroyed. Then he asks: "And who knows whether you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?"

Mordecai, Esther's cousin and guardian, speaks to her because Haman had obtained a decree to destroy the Jews. Esther feared approaching the king without being summoned, since that could cost her life. Mordecai trusts that God will not abandon his people, although the text does not name God.

For today: perhaps God has placed you in your position, job, or family to help someone. Do not wait until everything feels safe; ask in prayer what good you can do today, and do it with courage and humility.
exp.1:3:
This verse says that the king's servants propose a plan: to seek out beautiful young virgins, and whichever one pleases the king will become the new queen in place of Vashti. The idea seemed good to the king, and he put it into practice. Old-fashioned words: "maiden" is a young woman; "pleaseth" means pleased or delighted; "instead of" means in the place of.

The ones speaking are the attendants of King Ahasuerus (Xerxes). He had grown angry with Vashti because she did not obey his summons, and they look for a solution. It is a human plan, made for convenience and power, and many women had no choice. Here God is not named, but the book will go on to show how his care works quietly.

For today: even when we see unjust or selfish decisions around us, we can trust that God is still at work. In the meantime, let us ask for wisdom to treat others with respect and justice.
exp.6:1:
This verse tells that on the second day of the banquet of wine, the king asks Esther again what she wants to request from him. He promises that she will be granted it, even if it is half of the kingdom. "Request" means what she asks for, and "performed" means that it will be carried out.

The king Ahasuerus (Xerxes) speaks with Queen Esther. She had prepared a banquet and also invited Haman, the enemy of the Jews. On the first day the king had already asked her the same question, but Esther waited. Now, at the right moment, she will make known her petition to save her people.

For today: sometimes doing what is right requires patience and good timing, not only courage. Pray, ask God for wisdom, and wait for his guidance before speaking or acting in difficult situations.
exp.6:8:
Here the account tells how Harbonah, a eunuch who served the king, reports to him that Haman had had a gallows built about fifty cubits high, roughly twenty-three meters, for Mordecai, the man who had spoken well of the king. A gallows is a tall wooden structure used for hanging or impaling someone. The king answers: "Hang him thereon."

Harbonah speaks at the moment when Haman is already condemned because of his attitude toward the queen. Mordecai had earlier uncovered a plot against the king, and Haman wanted to kill him out of pride and resentment. Scholars do not know the exact height of the gallows, but the text emphasizes its excessiveness.

Today we can learn that the harm planned against others can turn back on the one who prepares it. Instead of feeding resentment, let us trust in God, who sees injustice and knows how to act in his own time.
exp.2:5:
He thought it too little to lay hands only on Mordecai. Since he already knew that Mordecai was a Jew, Haman decided to destroy all the Jews in the kingdom of Ahasuerus. Laying hands on someone means raising a hand against them to do them harm. Sought to destroy means that he looked for a way to accomplish it.

The book of Esther tells this from the narrator's point of view. Mordecai would not bow down before Haman, the king's high official, and Haman was filled with rage. His personal anger grew until it became a plan against a whole people. The text does not explain in detail why Mordecai would not kneel; some think it was for reasons of faith, but the Bible does not clarify this here.

Today, this verse warns us that wounded pride and resentment, if they are not stopped, can grow until they harm many people. When we feel offended, let us bring that anger to God quickly, before it leads us to do something unjust.
exp.3:1:
This verse says that Mordecai came as far as the entrance of the palace, but he could not go in. At that time no one was allowed to enter the king's gate dressed in sackcloth. Sackcloth was a rough, coarse cloth worn as a sign of mourning or grief.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Mordecai had just learned of the decree that condemned the Jews to death. That is why he showed his distress in public. His grief was so great that it led him to the king's gate, even though the palace, by custom, did not allow signs of mourning.

When something truly hurts us, we do not have to pretend we are fine. We can bring our pain honestly before God and trusted people, and seek help instead of carrying it alone.
exp.5:10:
Haman does exactly what the king commanded. He takes the royal robe and the horse, dresses Mordecai, leads him through the street of the city, and proclaims before him that this is how the man the king wishes to honor shall be treated.

The narrator is telling the scene. Haman had believed the king wanted to honor him, and that is why he proposed such a great honor. But the king orders that it be given to Mordecai, the Jew whom Haman hated and wanted to destroy. So Haman is humiliated in front of everyone.

For today: pride and resentment can blind us and turn against us. It is better to learn to recognize the achievements of others without envy, and to trust that God is the one who lifts up and brings down in his own time.
exp.5:3:
This verse shows the king, unable to sleep, asking who is in the court. Right there was Haman, who had come early to ask the king's permission to hang Mordecai on the gallows already prepared. Here "gallows" refers to a tall wooden post or pole, and "outer court" was the outer area of the palace.

King Ahasuerus is speaking. That night he could not sleep, and he ordered the book of the chronicles to be read, where it was found that Mordecai had uncovered a plot against his life and had never been rewarded. Haman arrives with his plan of revenge, not knowing that the king is thinking of honoring Mordecai. The two intentions cross at that moment.

For today: even when it sometimes seems that no one sees the good we do, God knows the right moment. We do not have to take revenge or rush things; we can trust that He governs the times and justice.
exp.2:1:
What it says: All the king's servants who were at the palace gate would kneel and bow down before Haman, because the king had commanded it. But Mordecai would not do so. "Kneeling" and "bowing" were gestures of honor and deep respect.

Context: The narrator tells how King Ahasuerus had raised Haman, the Agagite, above all the princes. The Bible does not explain here why Mordecai refused. Some think it was because of his faith, since the gesture seemed like an act of worship. Others connect it to the long-standing enmity between Israel and Amalek, from whom the Agagites may have descended. The following verses only say that Mordecai was a Jew.

For today: Holding firmly to what one believes can be costly and can bring pressure from others. Let us ask God for wisdom to be firm, respectful, and humble, while remaining faithful to Him.
exp.7:15:
The verse says that the Jews went through a complete change: they moved from anguish to light, that is, to hope and salvation. "Gladness" is a deep happiness, and "honour" means they were once again respected. One old word is "Jews," which today we write with a lowercase letter: Jews.

It is the narrator of the book of Esther who tells this. The king had allowed a second decree that let the Jews defend themselves, after Haman had planned to destroy them. Mordecai had been honoured, and the news reached all the provinces. The text does not name God, but many see in the story his hidden care.

For today: when God brings you out of a difficulty, do not keep the relief to yourself in silence. Stop, give thanks, and celebrate with others. And if today you are in darkness, remember that this story shows that sorrow can change.
exp.0:7:
This verse says that at King Ahasuerus's banquet, no one was forced to drink. The word "compel" means to force or pressure someone. The "officers of his house" were the people in charge of serving in the king's household. In other words, each guest could drink as much as he wanted, or not drink at all.

The book of Esther tells what happened in the kingdom of Persia. Here the narrator describes an enormous, very lavish feast that lasted many days. It shows the power and wealth of the king. This instruction about drinking was unusual, and the Bible does not explain why the king gave it. For that reason, it is best not to claim more than the text says.

For today: freedom and respect matter. No one should pressure others to do what they do not want to do, whether at the table or in life. We can make sure that the people who are with us feel at ease and respected.

sum.6: At the second banquet, Queen Esther asks the king to spare her life and the lives of her people, who were about to be destroyed, and she points to Haman as the enemy. The king becomes furious, Haman is disgraced, and he is hanged on the same gallows he had prepared for Mordecai. The passage shows how evil planned against others can turn back on the one who planned it.
sum.1: After the anger of King Ahasuerus had calmed down, officials searched for beautiful young virgins so that a new queen could be chosen. Esther, a young Jewish woman raised by her cousin Mordecai, was selected and won the favor of everyone who saw her. Esther kept her people a secret, just as Mordecai had asked her to. Mordecai uncovered a plot against the king and warned him, and this was recorded.
sum.4: Esther goes before the king without being summoned, and he extends his scepter to her and offers her up to half the kingdom. She only invites him to a banquet with Haman, and then to another the next day. Haman leaves happy, but his fury against Mordecai leads him to prepare a gallows.
sum.7: The king gave Esther the house of Haman, and Mordecai received the king's signet ring. Esther begged the king, weeping, to undo the decree against her people. Since the king's law could not be revoked, a new decree was sent out that allowed the Jews to defend themselves. There was great joy among them, and many people joined the Jewish community.
sum.8:
On the thirteenth day of the month of Adar, when their enemies had hoped to overpower them, the Jews fought back and won across the entire kingdom. They did not take the property of those they defeated.

Esther asked for one more day in Susa, and the ten sons of Haman were hanged.

Mordecai instructed that these days be remembered every year as Purim, with feasts, joy, gifts exchanged, and help given to the poor.
sum.3: Mordecai wept bitterly when he learned of the decree against the Jews, and through Hatach, Esther found out everything. She hesitated, because appearing before the king without being summoned could cost her her life, but Mordecai told her: "Who knows whether you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" Esther decided to fast with her people and take the risk: "If I perish, I perish."
sum.2: King Ahasuerus promoted Haman, but Mordecai, who was a Jew, refused to bow down to him. Enraged, Haman decided to destroy the entire Jewish people. He cast lots to choose the date and persuaded the king to sign a decree of extermination. The chapter shows how wounded pride can lead to terrible hatred, while the city was left shaken.
sum.9: King Ahasuerus imposed a tax on his land, reaching even to the islands of the sea, and his great accomplishments are written in the records of the kings of Media and Persia. The chapter ends by highlighting Mordecai, the Jew who became second only to the king. He was highly respected among his people because he sought their good and spoke peace to all of them.
sum.5: One night King Ahasuerus could not sleep, and when he had the chronicles read to him, he discovered that Mardochai had never been rewarded for saving the king's life. Haman, thinking that the man to be honored would be himself, proposed great honors, and the king ordered him to give them to Mardochai. Humiliated, Haman heard from his wise men that he would fall before this Jew.
sum.0: King Ahasuerus, who ruled over 127 provinces, held great banquets to display his wealth and power. When Queen Vashti refused to come before him, the king became angry and, on the advice of Memucan, issued a decree that she was no longer to come into his presence. The passage shows human pride and its consequences.
